pages.title: Purser
pages.description: AI-native, self-hosted personal finance — a double-entry ledger your agent can operate safely over MCP and REST.

pages.title: API-first design
pages.description: Why computation lives on the server, judgment lives in the client, and the web UI is only for administration.

sections.text: Purser is an agent's backend first and a web app second. MCP and REST are the primary interfaces; the admin SPA is a thin operator console over the same public API an agent uses. There are no private admin endpoints — which is exactly why an agent can do anything the UI can. The one deliberate exception is the page an agent's present link opens: it shows you rows in full and is for a signed-in person only.

sections.heading: Computation server-side, judgment client-side
sections.text: The dividing line is deliberate. Financial computation happens on the server; the agent normally provides interpretation and advice. An agent should never page rows and sum them in context to answer "how much did I spend on dining this quarter?" — that is slow, expensive, and error-prone. Instead every aggregate question has a dedicated tool that computes the answer in one call: spending summary, net worth, balance history, forecast balance, list recurring, list unmatched. The agent decides what to ask and how to narrate it; Purser does the arithmetic. Optional server-side AI categorization and review are exceptions to the default: they use the configured provider and documented review controls. The core works with AI disabled.

sections.heading: Token budgets
sections.text: Tool responses are budgeted. Aggregate tools return summaries, not row dumps , targeting well under 500 tokens for a typical answer, and no tool forces the caller to do cross-row math. This keeps answers cheap enough to ask freely and small enough to fit an agent's working context.

sections.heading: Three-tier answers
sections.text: Visualization-worthy tools answer in three tiers, so a caller takes exactly what it can use: 1. a one-sentence text headline — enough to narrate; 2. compact structuredContent — a declared, validated shape within the token budget; 3. a meta.ui.resourceUri naming a self-contained widget for MCP Apps hosts. Full-resolution series stay out of the structured payload behind purser:// resources, which share the same auth and are exempt from the budget. The read series tool returns the same series, byte for byte, to clients and gateways that forward tools but not resources — it shares the exemption, so it is read only when the compact answer is not enough. A host with no widget support still gets a complete answer from tiers 1 and 2. Every other tool also carries its answer as text, and an empty list arrives as [], so a gateway that rebuilds results from their text blocks never loses a "nothing found" answer.

sections.heading: Describe first
sections.text: Because the interface is the product, orientation is a single call. In every fresh session an agent calls describe first: one round-trip returns the data model, amount conventions, the caller's token scopes, the category tree, and the account list. The same guide is served unauthenticated at GET /llms.txt, and the search docs tool answers questions about operating Purser from this documentation.

sections.heading: Why the UI is admin-only
sections.text: The SPA provides account registers, schedules, positions, and an embedded forecast chart alongside setup, tokens, feed mapping, and review controls. Grafana supplies broader dashboards over the stable read schema. Both use the same underlying financial data and public interfaces. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md sections 1 (principles) and 10 (the MCP toolset and presentation layer).

pages.title: Balances
pages.description: Why a balance is recorded rather than recomputed, the three methods that produce one, and why you should never derive a balance by summing rows.

sections.text: A balance in Purser is recorded, not recomputed . Every surface that shows one — the register's Balance column, the account headline, the REST endpoints, the agent tools — reads a stored number rather than adding up transactions on demand. This page explains what is stored, the three ways a balance is produced, and the one rule that matters if you are an agent.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.text: Never derive a balance by summing rows. Purser already knows the answer, and summing a page of transactions cannot reproduce it: a page is a window, corrections supersede rows rather than editing them, and voided rows still appear in history. Ask for the balance you want instead.

sections.heading: Running balances are stored per row
sections.text: Purser keeps a running balance for every (account, transaction) pair where that transaction has a posting on that account. The number is the account's balance immediately after that transaction, accumulated in a fixed total order so it never depends on how a query happened to sort. That order is (date, created at, transaction id), ascending for accumulation and exactly reversed in the register. The transaction id is the final tiebreak because every row imported in one database transaction can share the same date and creation timestamp. Stored running balances and display order use the same canonical key, so same-day balances stay stable. It is derived data — rebuildable from postings at any time, never authoritative over them — but it is maintained transactionally : the recompute happens inside the same database transaction as the write that invalidated it. A reader can never observe a stale register. A nightly job re-checks the whole store against the postings and rebuilds if anything disagrees. Two consequences worth knowing: - A balance exists only for chain-head rows that are pending or posted. A voided row, a superseded correction, or an expected row has no running balance, and surfaces render it blank rather than repeating the previous row. - The same transaction has a different running balance in each account it touches. A transfer has two. This is why a balance is only meaningful from a named account's perspective.

sections.heading: The three methods
sections.text: What a surface reports as an account's balance depends on the account type, and every response says which method produced it via balance method (method on GET /accounts/{id}/balance). Method Applies to What it means --- --- --- postings checking, savings, cash, credit cards The stored running balance alone. valuation loan, property The latest valuation replaces the postings sum. A mortgage's feed reports a balance, not a transaction history, so the postings sum is not the debt. postings+holdings brokerage The latest holdings market value is added to the postings sum. Brokerage cash is real money the feed already reported, so it is not discarded. The holdings come from the feed's snapshots or, for an account tracked by hand, from its positions priced at the newest close. When an overlay produced the answer, balance as of names the date of the valuation or snapshot used, and postings balance carries the cash-only figure alongside. Closed accounts always answer from postings: closing zeroes the account, and a stale valuation or snapshot must not resurrect it. Net worth uses these same rules, so an account page and net worth agree.

sections.heading: Two bases, deliberately different
sections.text: There are two ways to ask "what is the balance", and they differ on future-dated rows: - As of a date — GET /accounts/{id}/balance?as of=, MCP account balance. Reads the stored running balance at that date and stops there. A row dated after as of is not counted. - Right now — the accounts list, the account headline, MCP list accounts. Includes every pending and posted row regardless of date, because that is what your bank's "current balance" means. Both apply the same overlays. The difference only shows up when the ledger holds a future-dated row — a pending charge that has not settled, or a scheduled entry you posted early. Forecasts start from the right now basis for exactly this reason: a future-dated pending row must not vanish from a projection.

sections.heading: Balance over time
sections.text: Because a running balance is stored per row, a balance history is a read rather than a computation. GET /accounts/{id}/balance/series?start=&end= returns one point per transaction that moved the account, each carrying the balance after it, the delta, and the transaction id to drill into — plus the opening balance carried into the window, so opening plus every delta equals the last point. The window defaults to the last 90 days. Points are oldest-first. Past 5000 points the response sets truncated rather than quietly dropping the tail. The same three methods apply, and the account type decides once for the whole window — an account does not change how it is valued partway through. The close cutoff, though, applies per date: history before a close keeps its overlay, and from the close date onward the account reads from postings.

sections.heading: Reconciled balances
sections.text: Reconciling an account records a statement balance for a date and posts one adjustment for any difference. It compares against the same chain-head rows the running balance uses, on a basis you choose: posted rows only, or posted plus pending. The claim keeps its target, so every read of the account re-checks it and reports a difference when a later write moved that date's balance. See Reconcile an account.

sections.heading: Recording a valuation
sections.text: A loan or property balance is its latest valuation. The feed records one for a synced account; record one yourself with POST /accounts/{id}/valuations, or from an agent with the MCP tool record valuation (both write scope), giving the date and the value on that date. Only loan and property accounts take a valuation. Any other account is refused with a 422 that says where its balance comes from instead: its transactions, plus its latest holdings snapshot for a brokerage account. To bring a checking, savings, cash or credit-card balance to a statement, see Reconcile an account. value is in the ledger's sign by default, the way Purser stores it: positive for something you own, negative for money you owe. To enter a loan figure the way its statement prints it, add "convention": "statement", and Purser negates it exactly as reconciliation does: Account On the date You send Purser stores --- --- --- --- Property worth 400000.00 "value": "400000.00" 400000.0000 Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "-250000.00" -250000.0000 Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "250000.00", "convention": "statement" -250000.0000 Loan 250000.00 owed "value": "250000.00" rejected with 422 A positive value on a loan is rejected unless you say it is the statement's figure: recorded as given, it would turn the debt into an asset in net worth. The answer's value is always the stored figure, in ledger sign.

sections.heading: For agents
sections.text: Ask search transactions with an account and each row carries balance — the same number the register shows, from that account's perspective. Without an account there is no perspective, so there is no balance field at all; with a category there is none either, since categories are virtual and hold no running balances. For a single point in time use account balance. For a balance over time use balance history(account, period) — one call, not a loop over dates. For a total across rows use spending summary. In no case should you add up amount fields yourself. balance history picks the density itself and tells you what it picked, so a naive call cannot blow your context: 30d is a true daily series, 90d lands on every third day, 1y on every fourteenth. low and high are computed over every day with activity in the window rather than the returned points, so they stay true even when the series is sparse — a low on the 19th is reported correctly by a series that never contains the 19th. movers names the biggest movements. Full per-transaction resolution is behind series uri, which serves exactly the window the tool summarized (for all, the whole history): up to 5000 points, oldest first, with truncated set past that. low and high are end-of-day balances: each day counts with the balance it closed at, never with a value it passed through on the way. Purser orders one day's rows by when they were recorded, not by when the bank processed them, so that order never produces an extreme. A paycheck imported as a gross pay line followed by its same-day tax and benefit deductions is not a high, and a duplicate charge reversed the same day is not a low. The per-transaction points behind series uri still show those intra-day steps. The three questions and their tools: Question Tool --- --- One account, over time balance history(account, period) Everything, over time net worth(period) One account, looking forward forecast balance(account, days) net worth(period="all") starts at the ledger's earliest activity but at most ten years back, and its series uri serves that same window day by day.

pages.title: Categories
pages.description: Why categories are hierarchical virtual accounts rather than tags, how the curated default set works, and how imports arrive already categorized.

sections.text: In Purser a category is not a label you stick on a transaction. It is an account — a virtual one — and categorizing is a real posting to it. That one decision is why spending rollups, transfers, and double-entry all compose cleanly instead of fighting each other.

sections.heading: Categories are virtual accounts
sections.text: There is no categories table. A category is an accounts row with is virtual = true, an income or expense type, and its place in a hierarchy given by an ltree path like expenses.dining.coffee. Because the hierarchy is an ltree, a spending rollup is a single indexed subtree query — everything under expenses.dining is path <@ 'expenses.dining', one query, no recursion in application code. A path is labels joined by single dots, each label made of letters, digits, and -. A malformed path such as expenses..dining or expenses.eating out is rejected with a 422 whose message names the offending segment, so a typo never reaches the database.

sections.heading: Why this beats tags
sections.text: A tag is metadata bolted onto a row; nothing balances, and a subtotal means scanning and summing. Making the category an account means the flat write { "category": "expenses.dining" } expands to a balanced posting pair, subtree totals fall out of the ledger itself, and a transfer is just a transaction whose "category" happens to be another real account. Categorization becomes a first-class ledger operation with an audit trail, not an editable sticky note.

sections.heading: A curated, described default set
sections.text: Purser ships 100 categories whose structure is adapted from the Plaid Personal Finance Categories taxonomy, with the transfer and loan-payment groups deliberately removed — those are structural transfers here, not spending. The set is seeded once and merges additively on upgrade, so your deletions stick. Every category carries a one-line description , in Purser's own words, written for the AI classifier and surfaced in the Config - Categories tab. The set is finite by design . You may rename, re-describe, and add categories, and delete any that are unused, but re-parenting and path renames are not supported in v1. The AI classifier picks from a closed list — the existing tree plus your own accounts in brackets (see below) — and can never invent a category. Agents have no category-creation tool, and creating a category is an admin-UI action, so the taxonomy stays curated rather than sprawling into a thousand near-duplicates. Category paths stay put — schedule templates store them — but a real account can move. PATCH /accounts/{id} with a new path moves it and every account beneath it, keeping their relative paths: a card created at citicard becomes liabilities.citicard. History and balances follow, because transactions point at accounts by id. A destination that another account already occupies is a 409. A destination under a category root such as expenses is refused, because subtree totals there would count the account's own postings as spending. Renaming a real account, in the app or with the MCP update account tool, changes only its display name and keeps its path, so tools, rules and outside integrations that refer to it by path keep working. The name still matters to matching: a bank row that mentions an account's name is one of the signals that links a transfer to it.

sections.heading: Born categorized
sections.text: Imports are not dumped in as uncategorized. A deterministic payee-to-category memory, learned from your accepted history, runs at import time : when Purser has seen a payee before, the new row arrives already categorized, and no correction is ever needed. The optional AI classifier handles only the misses. See design section 11 for that pipeline.

sections.heading: The bracket duality
sections.text: Because a category is an account, the "category" slot is polymorphic. Normally it holds a virtual category account. On a transfer it holds the other real account , shown in Quicken-style brackets like [assets.savings]. Same slot, same flat shape — a categorized expense and a transfer differ only in whether that slot points at a virtual or a real account. See Manage transfers for the write-side sugar. The optional AI classifier can use that slot too: your own accounts are offered to it as bracket options, so a transfer has a correct answer available instead of forcing a wrong category. A bracket answer is one-sided — it names the other account and leaves that side unbacked until the counterparty row arrives — and it must clear a higher confidence bar than an ordinary category, because it restructures the row and moves a second account's balance. Below that bar the row simply stays uncategorized. Collapsing two rows that describe the same movement stays deterministic and is never something the model decides. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md sections 3.2 (categories as virtual accounts), 3.3 (bracket transfers), and 11 (AI categorization).

pages.title: Forecasting
pages.description: Why Purser forecasts deterministically from schedules and running balances, with no statistical models, and how shortfalls surface.

sections.text: Purser's forecast answers "will this account dip below zero before payday?" and it answers it the same way every time. The forecast is deterministic : it is your current balance plus the expected transactions your schedules already imply -- not a prediction learned from a model.

sections.heading: Schedules plus running balances
sections.text: A forecast starts from a real, stored balance and walks forward, applying each expected instance that active schedules materialize on the horizon. The result is a daily series where every step is a named, dated event — the rent on the 1st, the paycheck on the 15th — carrying the running balance after at that point. The narration and the chart come from exactly the same data, because the events array is the chart.

sections.heading: No statistical models, by design
sections.text: There is no regression, no seasonality model, no machine-learned trend. That is a choice, not a gap. A deterministic forecast is explainable : every projected movement traces to a schedule you can inspect and edit, so when the number surprises you, you can see precisely which expectation caused it. A statistical forecast that is confidently wrong about your rent is worse than useless for planning cash.

sections.heading: Shortfalls
sections.text: forecast balance(account, days) (horizon defaults to 30 days) returns the daily series, the projected minimum (low), and the account floor (min balance, null when unset; the headline then measures against zero). Calling it only reads: it never emits an event. The warning comes from a nightly scan instead. At 07:15 UTC Purser forecasts the next 30 days of every open account that has a floor, and when a projection crosses that floor it emits a forecast.shortfall event, once per account and first shortfall date. The warning reaches you through the event stream, a webhook, or the whats new digest before the account actually runs dry, not after. An account without a floor is never scanned, so set one on every account you want watched. The floor is the account's min balance, a decimal string in ledger sign. Set it when you create the account (POST /accounts) or at any time after: the Set floor control in the account's register header, PATCH /accounts/{id} with {"min balance": "500.00"}, or the MCP tool update account(account, min balance="500.00"), so an agent can act on "warn me if checking goes under $500". Changing it needs the write scope, like a rename, and is audited as an account.update with the old and new floor. The next nightly scan uses the new floor. Clearing it (null over REST, "" in update account, Clear in the app) takes the account out of the scan, so its warnings stop. A credit card is negative when owed, so "warn me past 4,500.00 owed" is a floor of -4500.00; zero warns before an overdraft. Floors apply to checking, savings, cash and credit-card accounts. Brokerage, property and loan forecasts start from a market value or a stated valuation, so a floor there is refused (422).

sections.heading: Horizon semantics
sections.text: The horizon is a count of days forward from today, up to 365. Schedules materialize their instances on a rolling 60-day window; for slots past that the forecaster expands the rules on the fly, so a 180-day call still shows every occurrence. Those events are flagged projected — the rule expects them, but no instance row exists yet to edit or match — while events with a transaction id are instances you can skip, override or mark paid. An instance dated before today that has not been matched is flagged overdue: it lands on day 0, because it is still due. The uncleared rows of a file import are expected too, so an outstanding check lands on day 0 the same way until the matcher pairs it with the bank's posted row. A slot you skipped never appears, projected or not. The series stays daily, and the full daily series is always available behind a purser:// resource. An instance the matcher has already proposed a bank row for is treated as paid, pending your confirmation. That row — pending or posted — is already in the starting balance, so landing the instance as well would subtract the money twice. The forecast leaves it out, whether it is overdue or due within the five-day match window, and the line is exactly what confirming the match would give: the bank's amount, never a leftover difference. Reject the proposal and the instance is back on the next forecast; confirm it (in the register, or with match on the same pair) and it is settled for good. An account valued by a stated figure rather than its postings (a loan or property with a valuation) keeps such instances, because no bank row moves that figure.

sections.heading: Where each amount comes from
sections.text: Every event carries a basis: what produced its amount. A schedule's own amount is fixed, or the estimate it follows — last, rolling avg 3, rolling avg 12, or counterparty balance, which for a card payment is the card's current balance. An amount someone supplied is override (you pinned the instance with a different amount or date) or statement (a recorded card statement balance). The REST forecast and the full daily series carry basis on every event; forecast balance names it only for statement and override, the amounts an agent should be able to explain, and leaves it off the rest to stay inside its budget.

sections.heading: Estimate range
sections.text: An estimated amount is a point taken from history, and history varies. So an event whose amount a schedule estimates — a rolling average, the last amount, or a card payment's current balance — also carries a range: the lowest and highest of the schedule's six newest settled amounts together with the event's own amount, so the point always sits inside. A card payment's range is its past payments together with the card's current balance (not the balance's swing from zero to its peak over a cycle). It needs at least two settled amounts that differ; a fixed amount, an amount you overrode, and a recorded card statement have no range, because nothing about them is uncertain. When any event has a range, the forecast also walks the horizon twice more: once with every ranged event at its worst (outflows at their high, inflows at their low) and once at its best. Each day then carries low and high beside its balance, and the forecast reports the lowest point of each pass. forecast balance puts that under low.range — low and low date for the pessimistic pass, high for the optimistic one — and when only the pessimistic pass dips below the floor, the headline says which event would cause it: "It could dip to -125.00 on 2026-10-26 if Citi payment comes in high." The forecast.shortfall event stays on the expected amounts, so a wide range never raises an alert on its own. The forecast widget and the Schedules page chart shade the band behind the line, and an event's tooltip names its basis and range.

sections.heading: What the event list shows
sections.text: forecast balance keeps its answer inside a token budget, so its events list holds the movements that fit, not necessarily all of them. The movement that produces the projected low is always listed, then the largest by amount; pass materiality (a decimal string such as "100.00") to list only movements at least that large. Whatever is not listed is accounted for in omitted — how many movements and their net — and end balance is the balance on the last day, so start balance plus the listed amounts plus omitted.net is always end balance. truncated is true only when the budget, rather than your materiality, left a movement out, and the headline then says how many. Every day is in the series the payload's daily uri names: read it with resources/read, or with the read series tool when your client or gateway forwards tools but not resources. The horizon (days) is 1 to 365, and every horizon the tool accepts is one the series serves.

sections.heading: Coverage: what the line is made of
sections.text: Every forecast carries coverage: how many active schedules touch the account, how many instances and projected occurrences went into the line, how many open suggestions name the account, and matches pending — how many instances were left out as paid pending a match confirmation, with their net in matches pending net (a decimal string, present only when it is not zero). The headline names them too, so a caller knows confirmations are outstanding: list unmatched shows each one with proposed posted id, the bank row it was paired with, and match on that pair confirms it. A flat line with schedules active: 0 is not a calm month — it is an account with nothing modeled, and the headline says so instead of reporting that the balance "stays above its floor". Looking backward is the mirror image. One account's history is balance history(account, period), which reads the same kind of recorded running balance in the other direction — and has the same "the series IS the chart" property, except the numbers were stored rather than projected. Net worth over time is the whole-portfolio counterpart — see design section 8. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 6 (schedules and forecasting). The tool contract is in the MCP tool catalog under forecast balance.

pages.title: The ledger
pages.description: Flat outside, double-entry inside — why the books cannot be silently wrong.

sections.text: Purser's core promise is that the books cannot be silently wrong. Three mechanisms deliver it: a double-entry core behind a flat API, immutable posted rows with linked corrections, and an append-only raw feed the ledger can always be re-derived from.

sections.heading: Flat outside, double-entry inside
sections.text: Clients — human or agent — submit the flat form a person thinks in: { "account": "citicard", "date": "2026-07-01", "amount": "-14.00", "payee": "Chipotle", "category": "expenses.dining" } The server expands every write into a balanced posting pair (citicard -14.00, expenses.dining +14.00). Postings per transaction sum to zero per currency — enforced in the application layer with a database trigger as backstop. Reads return the flat view by default; full postings are available on request. Categories are themselves accounts — hierarchical virtual accounts with ltree paths like expenses.dining.coffee — which is what makes categorization a first-class ledger operation instead of a tag. A transfer is one transaction with two real-account postings; in the flat view its "category" appears as the other account in Quicken-style brackets, like [assets.savings]. A split loan payment keeps both bank legs exact and adds one interest/fee posting for the difference, so it still sums to zero — see Confirm a split loan payment.

sections.heading: Split transactions
sections.text: One bank amount spread over several categories is a split transaction : one leg on the real account plus one leg per category line, still summing to zero. It is never a transfer and never has a second real leg; money a split sends to another account is a transfer of its own. The flat view shows a split with no single category path and a split lines count, and the transaction's postings carry the lines. Split rows come from QIF imports today and are read-only.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and immutability
sections.text: Every transaction moves through expected - pending - posted - void: - expected — future entries: manual bills, materialized schedule instances, and the rows a QIF or CSV file marks uncleared. Estimates, consumed by the matcher and forecaster. - pending — rows the bank feed reports as not yet cleared, and manual or agent entries the bank has not posted yet. Freely editable. - posted — immutable . Any change, including recategorization, executes as an atomic reversal + replacement pair linked via reverses id. The flat view collapses the chain; the ledger keeps the forensic history. The database allows exactly one mutation of a posted row: voiding it with a lineage link in the same statement. - void — dead rows kept for lineage: superseded expecteds, merged transfer halves, vanished pendings, reversal legs. Nothing is ever silently edited or deleted; every correction is itself a visible ledger event with an audit trail.

sections.heading: The raw feed underneath
sections.text: Every payload a bank connection returns is archived verbatim, append-only, before anything touches the ledger. Feed syncs and manual imports are content-hash idempotent — re-running any import produces zero new rows. A row's identity is what the bank sent (account, date, amount, description) plus, for identical rows in one payload, which occurrence it is — so two same-day coffees at the same price stay two rows, and re-fetching or re-importing them adds none. Every ledger row traces to the source bytes that produced it, and the ledger is a projection that can be re-derived from the archive.

sections.heading: Where the invariants live
sections.text: These rules are enforced structurally — app-layer checks with database triggers as backstop, and property-based tests over the invariants (zero-sum postings, immutability, idempotent import). The authoritative specification is DESIGN.md in the repository — these pages explain the behavior; that document defines it.

pages.title: Matching
pages.description: Why reconciling expectations against imported reality is the center of gravity, and how candidates, tiers, and variance work.

sections.text: Matching is Purser's center of gravity. A ledger that only records what already cleared is a rear-view mirror; Purser also holds expectations — manual bills, materialized schedule instances, and the uncleared rows of a file import — and reconciles them against the imported reality of what the bank actually did. That reconciliation is where "the books cannot be silently wrong" earns its keep.

sections.heading: Expected versus imported
sections.text: An expected transaction is an estimate: the $60.00 gym charge you know is coming. An imported pending or posted row is what the feed reported. The matcher's job is to recognize that these two are the same event and collapse them into one truthful row — without ever letting the estimate overwrite what really happened.

sections.heading: Candidate scoring
sections.text: For each expectation the matcher looks at rows in the same account within a date window (default plus or minus 5 days), scoring normalized-payee similarity and amount closeness. Crucially, amount is weighted softly : a row whose payee and date agree but whose amount differs is still a confident match — it just carries a variance . That is deliberate. A subscription that quietly rose from "-9.99" to "-11.99" should still match its schedule, and the price change should be recorded , not hidden by a failure to match. Candidates are bank reality: imported rows, and any live transfer — the two-leg row the auto-linker (or your confirm) builds when both sides of a card payment arrive. Every row is scored through the account being matched : a one-leg import and a two-leg transfer are both "-500.00 on checking" from checking's point of view. An expected transfer (a schedule with a counterparty account) is tried from each of its two accounts, and two rows that name the same counterparty account count as agreeing on the payee — which is how the expected card payment pairs with a merged transfer that carries no payee.

sections.heading: Three tiers
sections.text: The score sorts each expectation into one of three outcomes: - auto — a high score matches automatically. - proposed — a middling score becomes a proposed match for you to confirm or reject. It waits as a match card in the suggestions inbox, and in the account register. Rejecting it is remembered: the matcher never proposes — or matches on its own — that bank row for that bill again, nor the posted row that replaces it. You can still mark the bill paid with it by hand. - unmatched — a low score leaves both rows standing.

sections.heading: Posted amount wins, and supersede
sections.text: When a match is made, the expectation is voided with a superseded by link to the posted row, and the posted amount is truth. The flat view collapses the pair to the single real transaction; the ledger keeps the forensic lineage. The matches row records the score and the variance, and that variance is not discarded — it sharpens future schedule estimates and, past a threshold, emits a variance.threshold event. A match can name a pending row, and pending rows are not final. When the feed replaces a pending with its posted row, a confirmed match moves to the posted row and a proposal is decided again. When the bank drops the pending, the match is released and the expectation comes back, because a dropped charge paid nothing. Voiding a matched pending yourself works the same way: the match is released (a proposal is withdrawn) and the expectation is due again. Estimates read only posted rows, and they read the current version of each: the posted successor of a pending, the transfer a row was merged into, the replacement of a corrected row.

sections.heading: Transfers whose sides post on different days
sections.text: The two bank legs of a transfer rarely post together, and the nightly job matches before it links transfers. When only the first leg has arrived, an expected transfer can settle against it — the matcher sees that leg from the account being matched, so it is a fair candidate (proposed when only the amount and date agree). That does not lock the leg away. A bank row matched to an expected transfer stays available for pairing, but only with a row on the transfer's other account, and when its counterpart arrives and the two link, the match follows the bank line into the merged transfer: a confirmed match simply moves, and a proposal is decided again against the merge, which agrees on accounts, amount and date. The expectation is settled exactly once, by the transfer, and the merged transfer — now matched — settles nothing else. A row matched to an ordinary bill never takes part. Unlinking the transfer releases what it settled, so the expectation is due again rather than settled by a row that no longer exists.

sections.heading: Unmatched, both directions
sections.text: The gaps are reported both ways, with aging: expected-but-missing rows are late bills, and posted-but-unexpected rows are new spending to triage. The list unmatched tool answers each direction, so an agent can ask "what bills haven't shown up?" and "what did I spend that I didn't plan?" as one call each. Transfer detection is a specialized branch of the same machinery — see Manage transfers. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 5, and the principle behind it is design principle 5. Correction history contributes only its current replacement. A reversal is an accounting entry, not a bank payment, and cannot settle an expected bill.

pages.title: Memories
pages.description: Short notes of financial nuance that Purser serves to your agent as context — and why they inform rather than act.

sections.text: Some things about your finances are not in your ledger. That the monthly transfer to a brokerage account is a child's 529 contribution. That one card is always paid from one checking account. That a recurring payment is a sublet, not rent. An agent cannot derive any of that from transactions. Memories are where you record it, and Purser serves them as context to whatever agent you connect.

sections.heading: Rules act, review flags ask, memories inform
sections.text: That division is the whole design. A memory never changes what lands in your ledger. No code path parses the text — there is no evaluator, no import hook, no scheduled job that reads one. The absence is deliberate: free-form text that acts would undermine the guarantee that only deterministic, user-declared boundaries decide anything. If a nuance should actually do something, it belongs in a rule. Rules can cite the memory that motivated them, and archiving that memory never disables the rule — rules are the executable layer and must not change behavior because a note was tidied.

sections.heading: Where they show up
sections.text: - describe() carries a count plus your pinned few, so a fresh agent session is oriented without pulling everything. - list memories fetches more on demand, filtered by account or payee. - The review loop attaches memories relevant to each row being reviewed. - The AI classifier , when configured, gets them as prompt context — which is what lets it act on "the monthly transfer to Fidelity is a 529 contribution" instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Relevance is exact, never fuzzy
sections.text: A memory reaches a transaction only when one of its links is that transaction's account, its category, or its payee. Foreign-key equality — no substring matching, no name similarity, no embeddings. A reviewer never receives a memory about a different account. Memories with no links are global and apply everywhere. One consequence surprises people, so it is worth stating: a memory linked only to a category cannot reach the classifier, because at categorization time the category is the thing being decided. Link to an account or a payee if you want the classifier to see it.

sections.heading: Drafts are never served
sections.text: When an agent records a memory it lands as a draft , unless you asked it to remember something. Drafts appear in Config → Memories for you to approve, and are not served anywhere — not in describe(), not in listings, not to the reviewer, not to the classifier. That is what stops an agent writing its own future context on its own say-so: a memory the agent decided to keep waits for your approval. The same gate applies to memories Purser writes itself, if you enable that. There are caps for the same reason: 500 characters each, 100 active, 8 pinned, and 25 outstanding drafts. The draft cap is the flood valve — nothing can fill your inbox faster than you can empty it.

sections.heading: Budgets, because context is not free
sections.text: A hundred memories is roughly twelve thousand tokens, which would swamp any agent's context. So serving is bounded at every width: describe() carries at most 8 pinned rows and 1,000 characters, list memories at most 25 rows and 2,500 characters, and the classifier prompt at most 5. Every response reports exactly how much it truncated, so an agent always knows what it did not see rather than assuming it saw everything.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Memory text is encrypted at rest alongside your payee names, descriptions and memos. Reading memories needs the read scope and writing them write. With the purchase-privacy setting on, payee names inside a memory's text reach an agent as references, like everywhere else (see Privacy and agents). An agent creates a memory as a draft unless you asked it to remember something: an active memory is context for every future session.

sections.heading: Archive, do not delete
sections.text: Archiving is reversible and is the normal way to retire a memory. Hard deletion is admin-only and recoverable only for as long as your audit retention window keeps the record — your own prose is not derivable from anything else in the system, so Purser makes it hard to lose. Purser never edits or archives your text on its own. A memory whose accounts were all closed is flagged stale and left exactly as you wrote it.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: - Write deterministic rules - Review new transactions - DESIGN.md section 3.6 and decision 48

pages.title: Privacy and agents
pages.description: How Purser lets your agent see only what a task needs — privatized defaults, include, payee references, and present.

sections.text: Everything an agent reads from Purser lands in its model provider's context. Your agent is your own and may see anything, but Purser lets it expose only what a task needs, the way an agent can use a password-manager secret without the secret entering the chat. There is no approval step: the agent chooses, the tool guidance teaches it to choose well, and your settings set the defaults. The authoritative spec is design section 9.

sections.heading: Two settings
sections.text: Both are in Config, Settings, under Privacy with agents , and both are off by default (PURSER PRIVACY PURCHASE, PURSER PRIVACY AMOUNT; see Configuration). Setting What an agent receives --- --- Privatize the purchase Each payee as a stable reference such as py 8k2mq4x7ra instead of its name. Descriptions, posting memos and bill (schedule) names are left out. Accounts and categories stay, because their names are yours and they carry most of the meaning. Privatize the amount No single-transaction amount: no row amount, no posting amount, no running balance (it would give each row's amount away by subtraction), no individual bill or forecast-event amount. Totals stay exact whatever the settings: spending summary totals, account balance, net worth, balance history series and the forecast's end balance. When an agent asks for a total, the total is the answer. Amounts are exact or left out, never rounded or made up: a number that is not true is something an agent might reason from or repeat. External account identifiers (the bank's account ids and connection ids) are left out for agents by default, whatever the settings: no agent task needs them. A call that passes include: ["external ids"] gets them.

sections.heading: Every omission is named
sections.text: A response says what it withheld, for example "withheld": ["amount", "payee"]. An agent that saw a field simply missing would conclude the value is unknown and might try to fix it.

sections.heading: Asking for a field: include
sections.text: A setting is a default, not a limit. Every tool that can return a withheld field takes include, any of payee, description, amount and external ids, and returns exactly those fields on that call. The audit log marks every call that asked for more than your defaults: open Audit Log and choose Agent disclosures beyond privacy defaults to see what your AI chose to see.

sections.heading: Working by reference
sections.text: Payee references and transaction ids work as inputs everywhere a payee or a row is named: search transactions(payee=...), update transaction, propose rule, match, memory links. Purser resolves them. A payee name you typed yourself is still accepted as a filter, because you disclosed it, not Purser; the answer stays privatized. A reference is never accepted inside free text (a description, a memo, a note, a name), so a reference cannot turn into a payee's real name. A reference stays the same when the encryption key is rotated, so an agent's long-term notes about it stay valid.

sections.heading: Showing you the details: present
sections.text: present(transaction ids, note) returns a link that opens those rows, with full detail, in Purser for you when you are signed in. The agent can reply "your four largest charges this week" followed by the link and the values never pass through its model. The link carries only transaction ids and the note.

sections.heading: What this is not
sections.text: These settings govern what Purser hands an agent over MCP. Purser's own web pages always show you full detail. REST serves full detail to any token that can read, except external account identifiers, which it leaves out for API tokens without admin scope.

pages.title: Security model
pages.description: Trust as a feature list — scoped tokens, attributable and reversible agent writes, full read and write auditing, sign-in throttling, and encryption at rest.

sections.text: Purser's pitch is that you can hand your agent your finances and know precisely what it did and what it saw. The agent is your own: it acts with your authority, and Purser makes every write attributable and reversible. That is not a promise, it is a list of mechanisms. This page is the map; the authoritative spec is design section 9.

sections.heading: Scopes
sections.text: Every token carries one or more scopes: Scope Grants --- --- read Every read tool and resource. write Every write: transactions, matches, transfers, rules, schedules, suggestions, valuations, holdings. admin Token and configuration management. The recommended default for an agent is read + write .

sections.heading: Undo, not pre-approval
sections.text: The safety net for an agent's writes is undo, not a review queue in front of every change. Posted transactions are immutable: a correction is a linked reversal pair, so nothing an agent does erases history. Every write is recorded in the audit log against the token that made it, and the register marks agent-made rows as agent-made. Proposing is the agent's choice per call. When it carries out your request, it writes directly. When it acts on its own initiative — a pattern it noticed, a rule it thinks would help — it proposes instead: a rule or a memory stays a draft that never runs or is served until you activate it, and a schedule lands as a suggestion for you to decide. A memory stays a draft unless you asked the agent to remember something, because an active memory is context for every future session. Every endpoint and tool declares the scope it requires; no route is open by default. The few that answer without a token are deliberate: first-run setup (until the first administrator exists), /healthz and /llms.txt.

sections.heading: What an agent sees
sections.text: Everything an agent reads lands in its model provider's context, so Purser lets you keep details out unless a task needs them. Two settings (Config, Settings, off by default) withhold payees and single amounts from agents; an agent asks for a field on a call when your question needs it, and the audit log lists every call that did. External account identifiers are left out for agents unless a call asks for them. See Privacy and agents.

sections.heading: No self-escalation for non-admin tokens
sections.text: POST /tokens requires admin scope. A non-admin agent token cannot mint a copy of itself or grant itself stronger scopes. An admin-scoped API token can create tokens , just as an admin's browser session can. Reserve that scope for trusted administration; it does not distinguish a human caller from automation.

sections.heading: Who can revoke a token
sections.text: Any token can revoke itself. A person signed in to the web UI sees and revokes every token of their own account on the Tokens page: their other sessions, and, for the admin, every agent token, since agent tokens are created under the admin's account. An admin-scoped token can revoke any token. Any other agent token sees only itself in GET /tokens and can revoke only itself. A request to revoke any other token gets the same 404 as a token that does not exist, so a leaked read-only token can neither sign the admin out, nor cut off the other agents, nor confirm that another token exists.

sections.heading: Reads are audited too
sections.text: Every mutation writes an audit log entry with the actor token, action, entity, and before/after — and so does every read . Each authenticated request writes one call row (REST via middleware, MCP via a tool wrapper that never logs credential material), and a shared request id groups a call with the changes it produced. The admin UI folds these into virtual sessions — per actor, split after 30 minutes of silence — so a long-lived agent token reads as conversation-shaped bursts. Audit retention is finite and uniform (audit retention days, default 90, floor 7), pruned nightly; the durable event stream is separate and is the permanent record for transfer automation.

sections.heading: Sign-in throttling
sections.text: Password sign-in is throttled against online guessing. Failures are counted per email and per client address: after five in a row for one email, or twenty from one address, further attempts are refused with 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header — before the password is even checked, so a locked-out guesser learns nothing. The lockout starts at 30 seconds and doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes. A successful sign-in clears its email's count; the address count only fades with time, so one valid password cannot cover a spray across other accounts. Every failed and every throttled attempt is audited (auth.login failed, auth.login throttled) with the email as entered and the client address — never the password. A refused sign-in never says whether an account exists. An unknown email gets the same 401 as a wrong password, and it takes as long: when there is no password to check, Purser checks the guess against a stand-in hash, so the response time gives nothing away either. The counts live in memory, per process: a restart clears them, and each API replica keeps its own. SSO sign-in and agent tokens never pass through it. The limits, and the proxy setting that lets the per-address count see real clients, are in Configuration.

sections.heading: Single sign-on
sections.text: SSO uses the OpenID Connect authorization code flow with state, nonce and PKCE, and validates the id token before any account lookup: an RS256 or ES256 signature from the provider's published keys, then issuer, audience, expiry and nonce. An SSO identity is the provider together with its subject. A provider's email links to an existing account, or creates one, only when the provider asserts it is verified, and an auto-created account is a member, never an admin. An account linked to one identity refuses another identity from the same provider until an admin unlinks it; a verified email moves it to a different provider. Emails match regardless of letter case. Only an admin can change the SSO settings, and password sign-in stays available whatever they say. The full list of checks is in Single sign-on with OIDC.

sections.heading: Requests from other sites
sections.text: The web UI signs you in with a session cookie, and a browser sends that cookie with any request to Purser, even one a page elsewhere triggers. So a write made with the cookie is refused (403) when the browser reports that another page sent it (Sec-Fetch-Site, or Origin). Reads, agent tokens and scripts are not affected. Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES), so no request, signed in or not, can make the server hold more.

sections.heading: Encryption at rest
sections.text: Encryption is required, not optional — Purser refuses to start without PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY, and a canary row binds the key to the database so a wrong key fails closed at startup. The model splits data into two layers. The narrative layer — the identifying words: payee names, descriptions, memos, schedule names, audit detail, event payloads — is encrypted. The numeric skeleton — amounts, dates, statuses, category paths, ids — stays plaintext, because every aggregate and invariant computes on it. Equality and dedup survive encryption through blind indexes and a keyed content hash, so a database dump cannot confirm a guessed transaction. The two hash keys are wrapped keys, which is what lets key rotation re-wrap ciphertext while leaving every index byte-identical.

sections.heading: The raw archive underneath
sections.text: Beneath the ledger, every bank payload is archived to raw fetches append-only, before anything touches the books — no code path may update or delete it. The ledger is a projection that can always be re-derived from those bytes, which is the last line of the trust story: even the ledger cannot quietly diverge from what the bank actually sent. See The ledger. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 9.

sections.heading: First administrator
sections.text: Complete setup before exposing a new instance to other users. The setup endpoint is intentionally unauthenticated until the first administrator exists. Concurrent setup attempts serialize through a PostgreSQL transaction lock, so exactly one can create the first administrator even when multiple API processes run. Later attempts receive 409 Conflict; a failed transaction releases the lock.

sections.heading: Reporting bugs and vulnerabilities
sections.text: - Bugs and feature requests: open an issue at github.com/mlamoure/purser/issues. Use synthetic data in examples; never paste real account numbers, tokens, access URLs or encryption keys. - Pull requests are welcome. Purser is developed in a separate repository and published to GitHub as one commit per release, so a pull request is not merged as is: the maintainer applies the change upstream and it ships in the next release. - Security vulnerabilities: report privately with Report a vulnerability on the repository's Security tab, never in a public issue. Fixes land in the latest release, the only supported version.

pages.title: Backup and restore
pages.description: Back up the single Postgres database, keep the encryption key safe separately, rotate keys, and run a restore drill.

sections.text: Purser keeps everything — ledger, append-only raw archive, config, audit — in one PostgreSQL database . Backup and restore are therefore ordinary Postgres operations, with one rule that matters more than any other.

sections.heading: The one rule: the key is not in the backup
sections.text: Data at rest is encrypted, and PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY is not stored in the database. A database dump contains ciphertext and the wrapped data-encryption keys, but not the master key that unwraps them. A backup is useless without the key. Record the key separately — a password manager, not the same bucket as your dumps — or your archived bank history is unrecoverable. This is the same key the setup wizard reveals once at install.

sections.heading: Back up
sections.text: umask 077 the dump is readable by you alone pg dump --format=custom --file=purser-2026-07-17.dump \ "postgresql://purser@db.example.com:5432/purser" Amounts, dates and account names are plaintext in a dump (see below), so keep dumps private: umask 077 before writing one, and a private bucket for copies. That single dump is the whole instance. Store the encryption key alongside your records of where the dumps live — never inside them.

sections.heading: What is and is not encrypted
sections.text: Encrypted at rest (ciphertext in the dump): the raw bank envelopes, SimpleFIN access URLs, webhook secrets, the AI and OIDC config secrets, and the narrative layer — payee names, transaction descriptions, posting memos, schedule names, audit before/after detail, and event payloads. Left as plaintext (the numeric skeleton every query computes on): amounts, dates, statuses, ltree category paths, ids, and the keyed content hashes and blind indexes that make dedup and search work over ciphertext. Encrypting the database files themselves is a storage and deployment concern, outside Purser's control.

sections.heading: Rotate the encryption key
sections.text: Rotate with the guarded CLI. Run with both keys configured — the new one first — so ciphertext re-wraps under the new key without ever exposing plaintext, and blind indexes and content hashes stay byte-identical: export PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY="<new-key ,<old-key " purser admin rotate-key Then drop the old key from the variable. See purser admin rotate-key for detail.

sections.heading: Restore drill
sections.text: Practice this before you need it: 1. Provision an empty PostgreSQL 16 database. 2. Before restoring into a fresh cluster, create the database owner/login used by the application and the read-model role: CREATE ROLE purser read NOLOGIN;. A database dump does not include cluster roles. If this role already exists, preserve it. Restore any separately managed reporting login configuration from your secure operational records; do not enable a new login by default. 3. pg restore --exit-on-error --dbname=... purser-2026-07-17.dump. 4. Start Purser with the same PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY set on the process (PURSER DATABASE URL pointing at the restored database). At startup Purser checks an encryption canary row that binds the key to the database: a wrong or missing key fails closed before serving anything, naming both fingerprints. A clean GET /healthz ({"status":"ok","database":"ok"}) confirms startup and database connectivity, not the completeness of a restore. Compare account balances and historical totals with the original instance, open encrypted descriptions, check record counts and raw archives, and verify that importing the same data again creates no duplicates. Do not treat health alone as proof that your financial data has been recovered.

sections.heading: Upgrade and roll back
sections.text: Upgrades move the database schema forward, and there is no downgrade. Your rollback point is a backup taken before the upgrade, together with the image you were running and the same key. 1. Note the image you run now (the exact tag or digest), and keep your key. 2. Take a backup (see Back up) and check it restores, ideally into a scratch database. 3. Change the image to the new version and restart. With Docker Compose, download the new release's docker-compose.yml (its URL carries the release tag, as in the Quickstart) over the old one in the same directory, keeping .env, then run docker compose pull and docker compose up -d. Migrations run automatically at startup. The API (serve) and the worker may start at the same time: they take turns on a database lock, so the migration runs once. 4. Check the instance as in the restore drill: balances, historical totals and encrypted descriptions match what you saw before. To roll back, restore the pre-upgrade backup into a fresh database (the upgraded one has the newer schema) and start the image you noted, with the same key. Anything written after that backup is lost, so schedule upgrades when no import or agent work is running, and take the backup immediately before. Agent tokens carry over an upgrade. A token issued with a scope that a newer version retired is converted to its replacement during the upgrade, keeps working, and the conversion is recorded in the audit log. The authoritative spec for the encryption model is DESIGN.md section 9; see also Configuration for the key.

pages.title: Connect an agent
pages.description: Wire an MCP client to Purser with a scoped token and the right operating conventions.

sections.text: Purser's primary interface is its MCP server. Any MCP client that speaks streamable HTTP — Claude, an OpenClaw agent, a custom runtime — connects the same way.

sections.heading: Endpoint and auth
sections.text: - Endpoint: https://<purser-host /mcp (streamable HTTP, same process as REST) - Auth: Authorization: Bearer <api-token — the same scoped tokens REST uses Create the token in the admin UI ( Tokens page) — the setup wizard also offers to mint one as its final step, with ready-to-paste config for the clients below. Recommended agent scopes: read + write . Scope Grants --- --- read Every read tool and resource write Every write, with your authority (audited and reversible) admin Token and configuration management (REST only) Your agent acts for you: with write it writes directly when carrying out your request, and proposes instead when acting on its own initiative (a draft rule or memory, or a schedule suggestion). Every write is attributed to its token in the audit log and reversible. Token minting requires admin — an agent can never create tokens, so it can never grant itself more access or clone its own. An admin-scoped token can mint tokens: reserve it for trusted administration.

sections.heading: First call: describe
sections.text: In every fresh session, call describe before anything else. One round-trip returns the data model, amount conventions, your token's scopes, the category tree, and the account list. The same guide is served unauthenticated at GET /llms.txt on the instance.

sections.heading: Operating conventions
sections.text: - Aggregate questions (spending, net worth, forecasts, unmatched) each have a dedicated tool — never page transactions and sum them in-context. - Amounts are decimal strings; negative means money out of the account. spending summary totals are positive-for-spend. - Accounts and categories accept a UUID or an ltree path like expenses.dining.coffee: dot-separated labels of letters, digits, and -. A malformed path comes back as an error naming the bad segment. - Bill emails: parse them agent-side and call create schedule or create transaction — Purser never parses email server-side. - trigger sync when the user asks for fresh data, not on every question — SimpleFIN Bridge allows 24 fetches per day. - Full series (forecast balance's daily uri, balance history's and net worth's series uri) are purser:// resources. A gateway or client that forwards tools but not resources reads them with the read series(uri) tool instead — same body, same auth, read scope.

sections.heading: Connect from your client
sections.text: Every client below wants the same two facts: the endpoint URL and the token. Substitute your host for purser.example.com throughout.

sections.heading: Claude (claude.ai and Claude Desktop)
sections.text: Open Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector and paste the server URL. Put the token under Request headers — header name Authorization, value Bearer <api-token (the whole value, including the word Bearer). The Request headers section is a beta feature still rolling out. If your account does not show it, the dialog only offers OAuth, which Purser does not implement yet — use Claude Code below, or any other client on this page.

sections.heading: Claude Code
sections.text: claude mcp add --transport http purser https://purser.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token "

sections.heading: Codex
sections.text: Codex (OpenAI's agent) shares one host config across the CLI, desktop app, and IDE extension: ~/.codex/config.toml (trusted projects can also use .codex/config.toml). The recommended form keeps the token out of the file by naming an environment variable: [mcp servers.purser] url = "https://purser.example.com/mcp" bearer token env var = "PURSER TOKEN" Export PURSER TOKEN where the Codex process can see it — GUI apps may not inherit your shell config. Restart the app or open a new thread so Codex rebuilds its tool list, then verify with codex mcp list. A literal http headers = { Authorization = "Bearer ..." } also works but stores the secret in plaintext config. ChatGPT web-chat connectors accept only OAuth or no authentication, so they cannot reach Purser yet — OAuth support is planned.

sections.heading: OpenClaw
sections.text: openclaw mcp add purser --url https://purser.example.com/mcp \ --transport streamable-http \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token " Or directly in openclaw.json under mcp.servers, with the token supplied via environment variable: { "mcp": { "servers": { "purser": { "url": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "transport": "streamable-http", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${PURSER TOKEN}" } } } } } Restart the gateway afterwards so the tools are picked up.

sections.heading: Gemini CLI and Code Assist
sections.text: Both share ~/.gemini/settings.json, so one command covers both: gemini mcp add --transport http \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <api-token " \ purser https://purser.example.com/mcp Or in settings.json (note httpUrl, not url, for streamable HTTP): { "mcpServers": { "purser": { "httpUrl": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${PURSER TOKEN}" } } } } The consumer Gemini app does not support custom MCP servers.

sections.heading: Any other MCP client
sections.text: { "mcpServers": { "purser": { "type": "http", "url": "https://purser.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <api-token " } } } } Clients that only speak stdio can bridge to the HTTP endpoint with mcp-remote. The full toolset is in the MCP tool catalog.

pages.title: Visualize with Grafana
pages.description: Point Grafana at Purser's stable read schema, import the shipped dashboards, and enable deep links on tool responses.

sections.text: Purser includes a forecast chart on the Schedules page and widgets for compatible MCP clients. Grafana provides broader reporting over a stable read schema, so your data remains available to dashboards outside the app. Three dashboards ship in the repository under grafana/dashboards/: - Purser - Monthly cash flow by category (purser-cash-flow) - Purser - Net worth over time (purser-net-worth) - Purser - Upcoming bills & forecast (purser-upcoming-bills)

sections.heading: The stable read schema
sections.text: The dashboards query a versioned readmodel schema — the query contract you can build your own panels against: View Feeds --- --- readmodel.v1 net worth daily Net worth, assets vs liabilities over time. readmodel.v1 spending by category month Cash flow by category and month. readmodel.v1 forecast daily Projected balances. readmodel.v1 holdings latest Latest brokerage holdings. readmodel.v2 transactions flat The flat transaction view. net worth daily is materialized and watermark-driven, so these read fast and stay current as new data lands.

sections.heading: Add a datasource and import
sections.text: 1. Create a read-only PostgreSQL role on the Purser database (the dashboards describe their input as a purser read connection). Reporting should never hold write access to the ledger. 2. In Grafana, add a PostgreSQL datasource pointing at the Purser database with that role. 3. Import each JSON file from grafana/dashboards/. On import Grafana prompts for the DS PURSER datasource input (labeled "Purser (PostgreSQL)") — select the datasource from step 2. The dashboards carry only grafana and postgres requirements, so no plugins are needed.

sections.heading: Deep links from tool responses
sections.text: Set PURSER GRAFANA URL to your Grafana base URL and Purser decorates tool responses with links.grafana deep links into the matching dashboard — so an agent's answer about net worth can offer the chart. When it is unset, links are omitted entirely. PURSER GRAFANA URL is runtime-editable in Config - Settings ; see Configuration. The design rationale for a shared read schema, built-in visualizations and external dashboard templates is DESIGN.md principle 7 and section 8 (net worth).

pages.title: Import QIF and CSV
pages.description: Load bank history from a Quicken QIF or CSV export with a mapping-first preview, per-account cutoffs, and content-hash idempotency.

sections.text: When an account has no SimpleFIN feed, or you want history older than the feed reaches, import a file your bank exports. Purser reads Quicken QIF and two CSV layouts through POST /import/qif and POST /import/csv — a two-step preview then commit , sharing one planner so every rule below applies identically to QIF and CSV.

sections.heading: Preview, then commit
sections.text: The preview is a strict, read-only dry run: it resolves your account mapping, suggests a cutoff and a sign per account, and returns the real counts it gets by checking content hashes against the database. Its per-account numbers equal what the commit will do for the same request — an exact rehearsal where only the commit writes rows. Adjust mapping, cutoff, and invert, then commit the identical request.

sections.heading: Mapping first
sections.text: Every file account maps to one Purser account. The preview drives the account selector (or inline account creation); a single-account file uses the parser's default name. For a multi-account CSV you can import a subset: set a file account's map value to null to skip it. Its rows are removed before planning and counted skipped unmapped, and any transfer whose counterpart was skipped degrades to a one-leg entry on the imported side. Per-account skip is a CSV surface (QIF's request map is not nullable), with one QIF exception: an investment account (next section) may simply be left out of the map.

sections.heading: Investment accounts
sections.text: Purser imports bank registers, not investment activity. A QIF file's !Type:Invst sections (buys, sells, dividends, share moves, and the investment side of transfers) are skipped and counted skipped investment in the preview and the commit, and the preview lists the account as brokerage. An investment account you leave unmapped stays out entirely: a checking transfer into it imports as a one-leg entry on the checking side, so the checking balance matches Quicken's. Map it only if you want those transfers as two-leg transfers into a Purser account; it then receives the transfers, never the purchases. A brokerage balance adds the holdings' market value to its postings (see the three methods), so importing the purchases as well would count every contribution twice. The investment section never books a transfer of its own, so a contribution no longer reaches checking twice either.

sections.heading: Cutoffs: manual owns the past, the feed owns the present
sections.text: Each mapped account may carry a cutoff date. A row imports only when its date is strictly older than the cutoff — the feed owns everything from the cutoff forward, so manual history and SimpleFIN never fight over the same days. The server never imposes a cutoff you did not send ; the preview only suggests one: the account's earliest feed-sourced transaction date minus a 3-day margin (QIF carries transaction dates, while SimpleFIN posted dates run 1-3 business days later), or null when the feed has not touched the account. This is the per-request twin of the persistent feed start boundary.

sections.heading: Sign invert
sections.text: Some banks export a card or loan file with spending as a positive number. A per-account invert flips every row's amount before hashing, category selection, payee memory, and transfer direction. The preview computes a sign diagnostic and pre-checks invert when a credit-card or loan target looks income-positive. Footgun: re-importing the same file with invert toggled produces a disjoint set of content hashes and therefore duplicates. The preview's skipped dedup count stays 0 across such a flip, which is the tell — watch it.

sections.heading: Transfers and the bracket convention
sections.text: A row whose category is another account in Quicken brackets ([assets.savings]) is a transfer, evaluated against both accounts' effective cutoffs: - older than both cutoffs - the two-leg transfer; - inside both - skipped (skipped cutoff), the feed owns that window; - split (older than one side, inside the other) - degrades to a one-leg flat entry on the older side, which the post-import auto-link pass then pairs with the feed counterpart (see Transfers). Zero-amount marker rows are structurally non-importable (the ledger rejects zero postings), so the planner filters them into skipped zero amount before hashing -- a $0 Quicken row can never fail a commit or half-form a transfer.

sections.heading: Split transactions
sections.text: A Quicken row can be split across several categories (S, E and $ lines; its category reads --Split--). Purser imports it as one split transaction: one leg on the bank account and one leg per category line, so a paycheck's gross pay and taxes, or a store run that was half groceries, land in their own categories. - A transfer line (S[Savings]) is taken out of the split and imported as an ordinary transfer to that account, which pairs with the savings account's own copy of the row in the same file. The money moves once, and the checking balance matches Quicken's. The preview counts these lines split transfers; they follow every transfer rule above, cutoffs included. - A line with no category goes to the uncategorized placeholder, never to the payee's usual category. If the lines do not add up to the row's amount, the difference goes there too, counted split remainders. - A split left with a single category line imports as an ordinary row. Split rows are read-only: they cannot be recategorized or edited in place, and neither the categorize pass nor a rule's apply-history touches them. A file imported before split lines were read landed each split row whole under expenses.split; importing it again dedups against those rows, so to get the lines, purge that import's batch first (purser admin purge-retired-rows, see the CLI reference) and import again.

sections.heading: CSV specifics
sections.text: /import/csv auto-detects two layouts by header row: an Amex activity export (Date, Description, Amount) of flat rows into a single account, and a Quicken CSV export (Date, Payee, Amount[, Category, Memo, Account, Clr, Scheduled]) where an Account column groups file accounts, a bracket Category is a transfer, and the Clr (or Cleared) and Scheduled columns drive the rules in the next section. When neither header matches, supply an explicit column map (date, amount and payee, plus optional memo, category, account, cleared and scheduled); until then the preview returns 422 csv layout unrecognized with the detected columns so a UI can offer a mapping form. Amounts are parsed as Decimal only (accountant negatives like (1,234.56) are read; float-looking garbage is a clear 422). CSV has no opening-balance convention, so mind any offset against a known statement balance.

sections.heading: Reminders and the cleared flag
sections.text: Quicken can include reminder rows in a CSV export: upcoming bills and deposits its register shows ahead of time, flagged in a Scheduled column. They are not history. The planner skips them, counts them skipped scheduled in both the preview and the commit, and never creates a row for them — model a recurring bill as a schedule instead. The file's cleared flag decides each remaining row's status: - QIF reads the C field: or c is cleared, X or R reconciled, and no C means uncleared. CSV reads the Clr or Cleared column, ignoring case: c, R, , X, Y, or the words cleared, reconciled, yes or true mark a cleared row; blank, N, U, or the words uncleared, no or false mean uncleared. Any other value is a 422, never a guess. - The flag counts per file account . In an account that marks at least one row cleared, an unmarked row is uncleared. An account with no marks at all — any bank-generated export, or a Quicken cash account nobody reconciles — carries no clearing information, so all of its rows count as cleared and import exactly as they always did. The same goes for a CSV with no cleared column. - Cleared rows land posted. Uncleared rows land expected and are counted uncleared: the bank has not seen them yet (an uncashed check), so they stay out of the balance — which keeps the balance-drift check comparing like with like — appear in the forecast (an overdue one lands today), raise bill.late like any unmatched expectation, and are settled by the matcher when the bank's posted row arrives. They never land pending: a feed sync voids any imported pending row it no longer lists, wherever that row came from. - A transfer lands expected only when no leg in the file is cleared; once either bank has seen it, it posts. A split transfer's one-leg entry follows its own leg, and opening balances always post. The preview's counts show both numbers before you commit, and the import page spells them out. When a later export marks a row cleared that an earlier import left expected, the commit posts that row in place instead of adding another, and the preview and the result count it promoted (once per leg for a transfer, which promotes when any of its legs is now marked). Only a mark promotes: an account with no marks carries no clearing information, and neither does a CSV without a cleared column. Promotion is limited to accounts without a feed — on a feed-connected account the matcher settles the row against the bank's posted row when it arrives, and posting it from the file as well would count that charge twice. Schedule instances and feed rows are never touched. Anything still expected can be posted by hand (POST /transactions/{id}/post) or voided.

sections.heading: Idempotency
sections.text: Both formats are content-hash idempotent over a shared qif: namespace. Re-run any import, or interleave manual imports with SimpleFIN syncs on one account, and you get zero new rows — the same history in either format dedups, expected rows included, and a reminder stays skipped. Identical rows are not duplicates. Two coffees on the same day at the same price are two rows in the file and two in the ledger: the second identical row in a file is the second occurrence of that content, an identity of its own. The count restarts in every file, so re-importing the file — or a later export that overlaps it — lands on the same identities and adds nothing. The same holds for transfers: two identical same-day transfers are two transfers, and so is a same-day round trip between two accounts. If an older import left only one row for such a pair, the next file that carries the pair adds the missing one, once. Both formats are raw-first: the verbatim upload is archived to raw fetches before any ledger write, and re-uploading an identical file archives nothing new. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 7.2.

pages.title: Deploy on Kubernetes with Helm
pages.description: Experimental. Install the Helm chart against an external Postgres with the encryption key in a Secret, review its locked-down defaults, and optionally split the worker role.

sections.text: Experimental: outside the supported release matrix.
