The Helm chart is kept and its defaults are hardened, but it has not been qualified against a real cluster , and releases are not tested on it. Docker Compose, in the Quickstart, is the supported deployment. Expect rough edges here. The chart lives in the repository at charts/purser. Its default image is the published ghcr.io/mlamoure/purser, tagged v + the chart's appVersion (for example v2026.10.0); to run your own build, push it to your registry and set image.repository. It runs the same one-image, multi-role design as every other deployment: an api Deployment (purser serve) and an optional worker.

sections.heading: Install
sections.text: The chart ships no encryption key, database URL or password, and refuses to render without them. Put them in a Secret first. The Secret must carry PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY and PURSER DATABASE URL; every other key in it also reaches the pods as an environment variable, so OIDC or AI-provider secrets can live there too. kubectl create secret generic purser-secrets \ --from-literal=PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY="$(python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate key().decode())')" \ --from-literal=PURSER DATABASE URL='postgresql+psycopg://purser:CHANGE ME@db.example.com:5432/purser' helm install purser charts/purser --set existingSecret=purser-secrets Record the encryption key somewhere safe (read it back with kubectl get secret purser-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data.PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY}' base64 -d): encrypted data is unrecoverable without it. purser keygen prints a key too. Instead of existingSecret you can pass secrets.encryptionKey and secrets.databaseUrl (plus secrets.extra for further secret variables), and the chart creates the Secret. Those values then live in your Helm release history, so prefer an existing Secret. Then port-forward to reach the first-run wizard, and connect agents to /mcp with a Bearer token exactly as elsewhere: kubectl port-forward svc/purser 8000:8000

sections.heading: Postgres: external or bundled
sections.text: postgres.mode chooses the database: - external (default): bring your own database through the Secret's PURSER DATABASE URL. It needs the ltree and pgcrypto extensions. For CloudNativePG, point the URL at the cluster's read-write service, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://purser:CHANGE ME@purser-rw:5432/purser. - bundled : a single-replica Postgres StatefulSet in the release, for evaluation only. It has no backups. Set postgres.password (16 or more characters of letters, digits and . ~ -; openssl rand -hex 24 gives one) or postgres.existingSecret. The chart keeps the password in its own Secret, and derives the app's database URL from it when you do not set one.

sections.heading: Secure defaults
sections.text: Every pod runs as the image's unprivileged user (UID and GID 999) with runAsNonRoot, a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, every Linux capability dropped and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. /tmp is a size-limited emptyDir; Purser writes nothing else to disk. No service-account token is mounted, because Purser never calls the Kubernetes API. The chart refuses to render when: - the encryption key or the database URL is missing; - a secret-shaped variable (one whose name contains SECRET, PASSWORD, TOKEN or API KEY, the encryption key or the database URL) is set under env, which renders as plain text in the pod spec: use secrets.extra or your Secret; - more than one scheduler would run (see the worker split below); - image.digest is not a sha256: digest. Value Default Notes --- --- --- image.repository ghcr.io/mlamoure/purser The published image. image.tag empty: v + the chart's appVersion The release tag format. image.digest empty sha256:... pins the exact image. image.pullPolicy IfNotPresent existingSecret empty Recommended. Needs PURSER ENCRYPTION KEY and PURSER DATABASE URL. secrets.encryptionKey, secrets.databaseUrl empty Required when existingSecret is not set. secrets.extra empty Further secret variables for the chart's Secret. env PURSER LOG LEVEL: INFO Plain settings for both roles. postgres.mode external bundled for evaluation only. postgres.password empty Bundled mode only; no default. api.replicas 1 Above 1 only with the worker enabled. api.resources requests 100m CPU, 256Mi; limits 1 CPU, 1Gi An idle API holds about 155 MiB. worker.enabled false worker.resources requests 50m CPU, 192Mi; limits 1 CPU, 1Gi An idle worker holds about 95 MiB. service.type ClusterIP ingress.enabled false networkPolicy.enabled false Ingress rules for the API and the bundled database. serviceAccount.automountToken false podSecurityContext, containerSecurityContext locked down as above Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB (PURSER MAX REQUEST BYTES), which bounds the memory an import can take.

sections.heading: Probes and migrations
sections.text: Every role applies database migrations when it starts, before the API listens. The startup probe calls /healthz and allows five minutes by default (api.startupProbe), so long migrations are not killed. Readiness also uses /healthz, which answers 200 only while the database answers, so a database outage takes the pod out of the Service. Liveness checks only that the server accepts connections, so a database outage does not restart the pod.

sections.heading: Optional worker split
sections.text: By default the API process also runs the scheduler. To split jobs onto a dedicated worker (same image, purser worker), enable it: helm upgrade purser charts/purser --reuse-values --set worker.enabled=true The chart then sets PURSER DISABLE SCHEDULER=true on the API pods, so only the worker runs jobs. Exactly one scheduler ever runs: the chart pins the worker to one replica, refuses api.replicas above 1 while there is no worker, and uses the Recreate strategy for whichever Deployment runs the scheduler, so an old and a new pod never overlap during a rollout. Both roles apply database migrations when they start. They take turns on a Postgres advisory lock, so pods starting together are safe: the second waits for the first, then finds the schema already current.

sections.heading: Ingress and TLS
sections.text: The ingress is off by default, and the Service is a ClusterIP on port 8000. ingress.enabled=true (with ingress.host, className, tls and annotations) exposes it. Set ingress.tls to a Secret holding the certificate, or terminate TLS in front of the ingress: ingress: enabled: true className: nginx host: purser.example.com tls: - secretName: purser-tls hosts: [purser.example.com] With an ingress, the chart sets PURSER PUBLIC URL to https:// plus ingress.host. That URL drives secure cookies, the OIDC redirect URI, and the host allowlist of the MCP endpoint, which rejects requests for any other host (HTTP 421). Set env.PURSER PUBLIC URL yourself when users reach Purser at another URL or through something other than this ingress. App settings go under env, which feeds both Deployments; a variable you set there always replaces the value the chart would derive. Every PURSER variable is documented in Configuration. Behind an ingress, every request reaches the pod from the ingress controller, so set env.FORWARDED ALLOW IPS (uvicorn's trusted-proxy list) to the controller's pod network. Otherwise sign-in throttling counts every client as one address. Throttle counts live in each pod: with api.replicas above 1, each replica keeps its own.

sections.heading: Network policy
sections.text: networkPolicy.enabled=true limits ingress to the API port to the peers in networkPolicy.apiIngressFrom (by default, pods in the release's namespace; add your ingress controller's namespace), refuses all ingress to the worker, and lets only this release's Purser pods reach the bundled database. Egress is not restricted: Purser calls your bank feed, OIDC provider, AI provider and webhook targets. The authoritative deployment topology is DESIGN.md section 2.

pages.title: Docker on macOS
pages.description: Run Purser in Linux containers on macOS; the published arm64 image is verified on Apple Silicon.

sections.text: Purser uses Docker Compose on macOS. There is no supported native macOS installer, Homebrew database installation, or Purser LaunchAgent.

sections.heading: Apple Silicon status
sections.text: Docker Desktop and Colima on Apple Silicon run Linux arm64 containers. Purser is built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, each natively on its own architecture, and Compose pulls the arm64 image on an Apple Silicon Mac. The published image is verified there: on 2026-10-28 it passed the release's end-to-end drills (onboarding, backup and restore, upgrade, crash and outage recovery, and failure journeys) on an Apple M1 with Colima and Docker, running natively with no emulation. Follow Set up Purser with your AI or the Quickstart. Docker runs both Purser and PostgreSQL. You do not need host Python, Node or Git. Keep the encryption key separately from database backups and retain the PostgreSQL named volume when recreating containers.

sections.heading: Restart and recovery
sections.text: Compose restarts containers while the Docker engine is running. Configure your Docker runtime to start when you log in if you want Purser available after a Mac restart. Purser does not install a macOS login agent. Use Backup and restore before upgrades. Never remove the database volume as a troubleshooting step without a verified backup. Purser is not published on PyPI. Do not install an unrelated package by the bare name purser.

pages.title: Track holdings by hand
pages.description: Record what a brokerage account holds when its feed sends cash but no holdings, keep those positions priced, and see how they reach balances and net worth.

sections.text: Some brokerages send an account's cash through SimpleFIN but no holdings. An employee stock plan is the usual case: the shares sit at the broker, the feed shows only the cash that leaves. Without holdings, the account reports its cash alone and net worth leaves the shares out. Purser can track such an account's holdings by hand. You (or your agent) record what the account holds, Purser prices it every day, and the value reaches the account's balance and net worth exactly like a feed snapshot would.

sections.heading: Switch the account to manual holdings
sections.text: An account's holdings come from one source at a time: the feed (the default) or positions recorded by hand. An admin switches a brokerage account, once: curl -X PATCH https://purser.example.com/accounts/<id \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"holdings source": "manual"}' In the admin UI the switch is the Holdings selector on the account page (admins only). - The feed keeps importing the account's cash transactions. It stops recording holdings for it: those rows are counted as holdings skipped manual in the sync result, and they stay in the archived fetch. - Feed snapshots recorded before the switch stay as history. The first hand-tracked snapshot is dated the day after the last feed one, so no date mixes the two sources. - Switching back to feed needs the account to be mapped to a feed account (a 422 otherwise) and changes no snapshot: the hand-tracked holdings stay in effect, so the account keeps its value, until the first sync after the switch ends the hand-tracked period. From that sync's date the account holds what the feed reports, and a position the feed does not report ends there (all of them, for a feed that sends only cash). The sync result counts what it ended (manual period tombstones), and the audit log records it as account.manual period end. The hand-tracked history before stays, and so do your positions and their events, read-only, until the account is switched to manual again. Unmapping or closing the account before that sync ends the period the same day; remapping it onto another feed account does not (that mapping's first sync ends it). If no sync of the account arrives for the price staleness threshold (7 days by default), the daily price job reports it once (holding.period open, and a whats new line): the hand-tracked holdings are still counted, unpriced by anything new, so check the connection or the account's mapping. Only brokerage accounts take a holdings source.

sections.heading: Record what the account holds
sections.text: "I hold 412.5 shares of ACME as of 2026-10-14" is one call. From an agent: record position(account="assets.plan", symbol="ACME", quantity="412.5", as of="2026-10-14", source note="broker holdings page, 2026-10-14") Over REST, open the position with its opening quantity: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/accounts/<id /positions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"symbol": "ACME", "quantity": "412.5", "as of": "2026-10-14"}' In the admin UI, the account page gains a Positions tab with + position and a Set quantity editor on every row. - quantity is a decimal string, up to 6 places. cost basis (optional) is the TOTAL basis of that quantity; with it, positions report an unrealized gain. Left out, a re-count of the same number of shares keeps the basis, a changed count makes it unknown, and zero shares have a basis of zero. The Set quantity editor sends a basis only when you type one; the field shows the current basis as a hint. - as of is today or earlier. A backdated quantity re-values history from that date, and net worth heals by itself. - Writes need write scope. A position has no draft state: a record is final, and a correction is a new event.

sections.heading: Buys, sells and corrections
sections.text: A position's history is a list of events: Event Means --- --- set quantity The account holds exactly this many shares on that date. buy It gained this many shares; with a price, the cost basis grows by quantity × price + fees. sell It lost this many shares; the basis drops at average cost. curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/positions/<position id /events \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"kind": "sell", "occurred on": "2026-10-01", "quantity": "20", "price": "101.25"}' Every write is checked against the whole history: a backdated sell that would leave the position below zero on any later date is refused (422), naming that date. An event dated in the future is refused too; record it once it has happened. Events are never edited. To correct one, reverse it (POST /position-events/<id /reverse) and record the right one with "replaces": "<id " (same date). The correction then takes the reversed event's place in that day. Without replaces, a new event goes after every event already recorded that day: re-recording an opening count after a buy on the same day would apply the count last and drop the buy. A position that holds nothing can be closed (PATCH /positions/<id with {"closed": true}, or Close on its row in the Positions tab); a closed position is read-only history. A position that holds nothing is not fetched, flagged stale or listed in the price status even before you close it. A new position in the same symbol starts after the closed one's last date (an earlier date is refused, 409), so the same shares are never counted twice.

sections.heading: Prices
sections.text: Each position is valued at the newest close for its symbol, from three sources: 1. a close you record: record price(symbol, date, close) or POST /prices; 2. the daily provider fetch, when a provider is configured; 3. a price implied by a feed snapshot of the same symbol in another account (its market value over its quantity). The newest date wins. The order above only breaks a tie between closes of the same date, so a close you recorded months ago never outlives newer ones. A feed-implied price is dated by the day the bank was fetched, not the trading session it reflects, so it ranks lower: it wins over a close you recorded or the provider's only when that close is more than seven days older. And while the bank keeps reporting the same value, the price keeps the date it first appeared, so a bank whose value is frozen turns stale like any other price. A position with no price at all adds nothing to the balance, and the surfaces say so (no price in list holdings, "no price" in the UI). It is never counted as zero. Neither does a position whose value at its close is too large to store, which almost always means a mistyped share count: the surfaces flag it as value out of range ("check the share count" in the UI), and recording a close does not change it; correct the count instead.

sections.heading: Configure a provider
sections.text: Config - Prices sets the provider, its API key and the staleness threshold: - Provider : none (the default: record closes by hand) or tiingo (end-of-day closes; a free key is enough). The provider sees ticker symbols only, never quantities, accounts or values. - API key : write-only and encrypted in Purser's database. There is no environment variable for it, and it never appears in a response or a log. A key with a space, a line break or a non-ASCII character is refused when you save it. - Stale after : a position whose newest close is older than this many days (default 7) is flagged stale. The fetch runs daily at 06:40 UTC. It fetches every date your positions hold shares (from a week before each position's first day, so a weekend start gets the Friday close) that the provider has not answered yet, including positions you have closed, and later only what is new. When the history grows (you backdate an event, or another account held the symbol at another time), the next run fetches the missing dates, wherever they fall. Dates the provider has nothing for (before a symbol listed, a weekend) are asked for once. Fetch now runs the same job on demand. One failing ticker, or one failing date range, never blocks the others: it records a price.fetch failed event and the rest carry on. Tiingo spells share classes with a dash, so a position recorded as BRK.B is fetched as BRK-B.

sections.heading: Price a plan-only fund
sections.text: Some plans' feeds send a fund they hold but cannot value: an employer plan's collective trust, say, which no market-data provider prices. The feed reports the shares with a market value of 0, or with none at all, so the position would add nothing to the balance. You do not need to track that account by hand for it: record the fund's unit price, and Purser values the feed's row from it on read. record price(symbol="ACMEX", date="2026-10-16", close="23.4") or over REST: curl -X POST https://purser.example.com/prices \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"symbol": "ACMEX", "date": "2026-10-16", "close": "23.4"}' - Record the price under the fund's ticker. The feed's symbol is matched the way Purser stores a ticker (spaces trimmed, upper case), so acmex in the feed takes the price recorded for ACMEX. - A feed that sends a description instead of a ticker (Stable Value Trust, say) cannot be priced: no recorded price matches it. Such a position is flagged unpriceable (in list holdings, GET /holdings and whats new) and adds nothing; there is nothing to record for it. - Any feed row of that symbol that holds shares with no value (0 or none) is worth shares × the newest price dated on or before the row's date. A price you record wins over a provider's of the same date. The feed's stored row never changes, and a value the feed does send is never overridden. - Recording a price for an earlier date re-values the account's history from that date; net worth heals by itself. - Weekly is enough: the newest price carries forward, and once it is older than the staleness threshold (Config, Prices) the fund is reported stale like a hand-tracked one: stale in list holdings, a price.stale event, Config - Prices and whats new's stale prices. - Until a price exists, the position shows no price (no price in list holdings, market value null), never a silent 0, and whats new reports it once (unpriced holdings). - No provider is asked for such a symbol: the price comes from the plan's site.

sections.heading: Where the value shows up
sections.text: Hand-tracked positions are written into the same holdings snapshots table the feed fills, so everything that reads holdings picks them up unchanged: - the account's balance is its cash plus its holdings' market value (balance method: "postings+holdings"), on every account surface; - net worth, balance history and the Grafana dashboards include it; - list holdings lists each brokerage account with its source, its value, and how many positions are on a stale close (stale price) or have no price (no price); named one account, it pages through its positions with their cost basis, in symbol order (cursor, next cursor). A page never repeats a position, but each page reads the account's newest set when it is called: a position added meanwhile with a symbol before the cursor is not listed, and the daily price job can move later pages to a newer set; - whats new reports symbols whose price turned stale (stale prices) and feed positions no price values yet (unpriced holdings). See Balances for how the postings and holdings figures combine, and Events and webhooks for position.updated, price.stale, price.fetch failed and holding.unpriced.

pages.title: Single sign-on with OIDC
pages.description: Wire Purser to a generic OpenID provider (Authentik as the example) with three runtime-editable settings that can never lock you out.

sections.text: Purser can authenticate admins against any generic OpenID Connect provider. Authentik is the worked example below, but the three settings are standard OIDC and apply to any compliant provider.

sections.heading: Register Purser with your provider
sections.text: Create an OAuth2/OpenID application in your provider (a confidential client, authorization code flow) and set its redirect URI to, exactly, your PURSER PUBLIC URL followed by /auth/oidc/callback. The redirect base is your instance's PURSER PUBLIC URL — which is environment-only, since it also drives cookie security. If PURSER PUBLIC URL is https://purser.example.com, register https://purser.example.com/auth/oidc/callback. Note the client id and client secret your provider issues.

sections.heading: The three settings
sections.text: Set the issuer, client id, and client secret. SSO enables only when all three are present : Setting Value --- --- PURSER OIDC ISSUER Your provider's issuer URL (e.g. an Authentik application's OpenID configuration base). PURSER OIDC CLIENT ID The client id from the provider. PURSER OIDC CLIENT SECRET The client secret (write-only: encrypted at rest, never echoed back, masked to set/unset in audit rows). These are runtime-editable in Config - Settings (or the admin-scoped /config API); the environment values are just the bootstrap default, and a database override wins. Every change is audited.

sections.heading: Who gets in
sections.text: An SSO identity is the provider's issuer together with the subject (sub) it issues: the same subject at another provider is another person. An identity already linked to a Purser user signs straight in. Otherwise Purser looks for an account with the id token's email, ignoring letter case, and only when the provider asserts email verified in the id token. An unverified email is refused: a provider that issues tokens with subject-chosen emails must not be able to take over a local account. The account with that email What happens --- --- Is not linked to SSO It links to this identity on first sign-in (audited user.link oidc). Is linked through another provider It relinks to this identity (audited user.link oidc, with the previous issuer). This is how you move to a new provider. Is linked to another subject of this provider Refused with 403 "this account is linked to a different SSO identity; ask an administrator to unlink it", and audited user.link oidc refused. Nothing changes. Does not exist Refused with "account not provisioned" by default. Pre-create the user in the admin UI (matching the verified email), or set PURSER OIDC AUTO PROVISION (also runtime-editable) to auto-create member accounts, again only for verified emails. email verified must be the JSON boolean true; a string "true" counts as unverified. An account stays linked to its identity: a later change of email at the provider does not move it. So only connect a provider that verifies the emails it marks as verified. Emails match regardless of letter case everywhere: SSO linking, auto-provisioning, password sign-in and the rule that every account has its own email. Purser keeps each email as it was entered.

sections.heading: Unlink an SSO identity
sections.text: When someone's identity at your provider changes (a recreated account, a new subject), Purser refuses it until an admin unlinks the old one. On the Users page, choose Unlink SSO on that user's row; over the API it is DELETE /users/{user id}/oidc with an admin token. The account, its password if it has one, and its history stay; the next SSO sign-in that asserts the account's verified email links it again. The unlink is audited user.unlink oidc with the admin as actor. Unlinking a user who has no SSO link answers 409. Links made before Purser recorded the provider were attributed to the provider configured at upgrade time. If none was configured then, such a link counts as belonging to whichever provider is configured now: its own subject signs in and records the provider, and any other subject is refused until you unlink it.

sections.heading: Move to another provider
sections.text: 1. Make sure the new provider asserts verified emails that match your Purser accounts (letter case does not matter). 2. Change the issuer, client id and client secret in Config - Settings . 3. Each person signs in through the new provider once. Their account relinks to the new identity, audited with the previous issuer. Accounts nobody signs in with stay linked to the old provider until they do, or until an admin unlinks them. Moving back to a provider you used before works the same way.

sections.heading: What Purser checks
sections.text: Each sign-in is an authorization code flow with three per-attempt secrets, kept in a short-lived cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, ten minutes). When PURSER PUBLIC URL is https://, it is Host-purser oidc state with Secure and Path=/: browsers accept that prefix only from this exact host, so a sibling subdomain cannot plant a sign-in attempt of its own. On plain HTTP, where the prefix is unavailable, it is purser oidc state, scoped to /auth/oidc. - state ties the provider's redirect back to the browser that started the sign-in, so a link to someone else's callback is refused. - nonce must come back unchanged inside the id token. - PKCE (S256): the code exchange carries the verifier, so a code seen in transit is useless on its own. The provider's discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration under the issuer) must name the issuer you configured; a trailing slash is the only difference allowed. When the issuer is https://, its authorization, token and JWKS endpoints must be https:// too. Discovery and the signing keys are fetched for every sign-in, so a key rotation at the provider takes effect at once. Every request to the provider has a 10-second timeout and does not follow redirects. The id token from the token endpoint must then pass: Check Rule --- --- Signature RS256 or ES256, by a key from the provider's JWKS selected by kid (a token without a kid is accepted only when the JWKS has one key). none, the HMAC algorithms and any other algorithm are refused, as is a key published for encryption or of the wrong type. iss Equal to the discovery document's issuer. aud / azp aud contains the client id. A token for several audiences needs azp equal to the client id; any azp must be the client id. exp Required; the token is refused once it has expired, with no grace period. iat, nbf iat is required. Up to 60 seconds of clock difference with the provider is tolerated for a token stamped slightly in the future. sub, nonce sub is a non-empty string; nonce matches this sign-in. email Required, a string. Unknown header parameters are ignored unless the token lists them in crit.

sections.heading: When sign-in fails
sections.text: The callback answers with a fixed message and logs the failing check, never a code or token: Status Meaning --- --- 400 The state did not match (an expired, missing or foreign sign-in attempt), the callback had no code, or the provider reported an error such as a cancelled sign-in. Start again from the login page. 401 The id token failed one of the checks above. The log line oidc.id token rejected names which. 403 The token was valid but Purser refused the account (see "Who gets in"). 502 The provider could not be reached, or answered something unusable: discovery, the JWKS or the token exchange failed (log line oidc.provider error, with the step). A wrong client secret shows up here.

sections.heading: It can never lock you out
sections.text: OIDC is safe to edit live. The OIDC client is rebuilt per request and password login is always available as an independent fallback , so a wrong issuer or a bad secret cannot lock the admin out — you log in with a password and fix the value. An explicit null override on the issuer or client id is the kill switch: it disables SSO even when the environment configures it.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.text: With all three set, the login page offers an SSO button that redirects to your provider and back through the callback URI above. If the round trip fails, log in with a password, open Config - Settings , and re-check the issuer URL and the redirect URI registered at the provider — those two are the usual culprits. The authoritative spec is DESIGN.md section 9 (security model); every setting is listed in Configuration.

pages.title: Reconcile an account
pages.description: Match an account to its statement balance, see what Purser posts and records, and how a reconciliation stays honest when history changes afterwards.

sections.text: Reconciling tells Purser "the statement says this account held X at the end of this date". Purser compares X with its own balance for that date, posts one adjustment for any difference, and records the claim. From then on, every read of the account re-checks the claim, so a reconciled balance never goes stale silently.

sections.heading: Which accounts
sections.text: Checking, savings, cash and credit-card accounts. These are the accounts whose balance is the sum of their transactions. Loan and property balances are valuations, and a brokerage balance includes market value, so their statements are not reconciled this way. Record a valuation for a loan or property instead, with POST /accounts/{id}/valuations or the MCP tool record valuation (see Recording a valuation). Reconciling a credit card checks what the card owed on the statement date; it does not change what you plan to pay. To make the upcoming card payment the statement balance, record it on the payment instead (see Card statement balances).

sections.heading: Enter the balance as the statement shows it
sections.text: Pass statement balance exactly as it is printed, and Purser converts it: Account The statement shows You enter Purser's ledger balance --- --- --- --- Checking, savings, cash 1250.00 in the account "1250.00" 1250.0000 Credit card 425.00 owed "425.00" -425.0000 Credit card a 10.00 credit balance "-10.00" 10.0000 Purser keeps a card's balance negative when you owe money, so a statement's positive amount owed is negated on the way in. Every amount in the answer is in the ledger's sign, except statement balance, which echoes what you entered.

sections.heading: Pick the basis
sections.text: Banks report one of two balances, so say which one the statement shows: - posted (the default) counts cleared transactions only. This is the usual statement balance. - pending inclusive also counts pending transactions. It matches the "current balance" many banking sites show. A pending hold dated before the statement date counts in pending inclusive and not in posted.

sections.heading: Preview, then reconcile
sections.text: POST /accounts/{id}/reconcile needs write scope. Start with a dry run. It runs the same computation, conflicts included, and writes nothing: { "as of": "2026-09-30", "statement balance": "1250.00", "basis": "posted", "dry run": true } { "reconciliation id": null, "account id": "3f6c1e52-1b1e-4c55-9a7e-0b8f5d2a7c41", "as of": "2026-09-30", "basis": "posted", "statement balance": "1250.0000", "target balance": "1250.0000", "ledger balance": "1225.0000", "adjustment": "25.0000", "adjustment tx id": null, "category": "expenses.reconciliation adjustments", "reconciled through": "2026-09-30", "created": false, "dry run": true } ledger balance is Purser's balance on that date before any adjustment, and adjustment is what it will post. If the adjustment is not what you expect, look for a missing or duplicated transaction before you commit. Then send the same body without dry run. The answer is the same, with created: true and the new ids. as of is the statement date, today (UTC) or earlier. A future date is rejected.

sections.heading: What Purser records
sections.text: - One adjustment, when needed. A difference becomes one ordinary posted transaction dated on the statement date, in the category expenses.reconciliation adjustments, with the payee "Balance reconciliation". It lands in the unreviewed set, so you see every adjustment, including one an agent made. If you later find what it was, recategorize it like any other transaction. The account balance does not change. - A clean reconcile too. When the ledger already matches, nothing is posted, and the reconciliation is still recorded with an adjustment of 0. - The marker. The account's reconciled through moves to the statement date. - An audit row and an event. Every reconciliation writes an audit row and emits account.reconciled.

sections.heading: When history changes later
sections.text: A transaction dated on or before a reconciled date can still arrive or change after you reconcile: a late import, an edit or correction, or a pending hold that disappears. Purser does not rewrite the reconciliation when that happens. It re-checks the claim every time you read it: - GET /accounts/{id} (and the accounts list) carries reconciliation, the latest reconciliation with ledger balance (the balance on that date now), difference (ledger balance minus target) and in balance. - GET /accounts/{id}/reconciliations lists every reconciliation, newest first, each re-checked the same way. - The agent tool list accounts carries the same check for each reconciled account. For example, you reconcile September 30 to 1250.00, and then a 10.00 deposit dated September 29 imports late. The reconciliation now reads "in balance": false, "difference": "10.0000". To resolve it, find the change. If it was entered by mistake, correct it, and the reconciliation reads in balance again. If it is real, the adjustment posted at the time was probably standing in for it. Reconcile the next statement: its adjustment nets the difference out, and the older reconciliation stays visible as out of balance.

sections.heading: Retries and conflicts
sections.text: Retrying is safe. The same date, balance and basis returns the recorded result with created: false while the ledger still matches. Once the ledger has moved, the retry fails with 409 instead of looking like a success. The response body detail says why: detail.code Meaning --- --- reconciliation moved This reconciliation is recorded, but the balance on that date has changed since. detail.difference is the ledger balance minus the target. reconciliation conflict A different balance or basis is already recorded for that date. Each account has at most one reconciliation per date. reconciliation out of order The date is before the account's latest reconciliation. Reconcile that date or a later one.

sections.heading: For agents
sections.text: The MCP tool reconcile account takes the same inputs and needs write scope. account is a UUID or a path: { "account": "liabilities.card", "as of": "2026-09-30", "statement balance": "425.00", "dry run": true } Do a dry run first, read adjustment back to the user, and commit only when they agree. Never flip a card statement's sign yourself. Purser does that. A loan or property statement is not reconciled. Record its figure with the MCP tool record valuation (write scope), entered as printed, with convention set to statement: { "account": "liabilities.mortgage", "as of": "2026-09-30", "value": "250000.00", "convention": "statement" } Purser stores -250000.0000, the ledger sign of an amount owed, and reports it as the loan's balance from then on. Without convention, value is read in the ledger's sign, so a positive figure on a loan is refused rather than recorded as an asset. Here too, never flip the sign yourself. The design and its trade-offs are in DESIGN.md section 3.7 and decision 61.

pages.title: Review new transactions
pages.description: Rows that arrive without human eyes form an unreviewed set over your registers — how to work through it yourself, with an agent, or automatically.

sections.text: Some rows land in your ledger without anyone looking at them: transactions the SimpleFIN feed imports, and transfers Purser merges on its own. Those form the unreviewed set . It is a filter over your existing registers, not a second inbox. Purser deliberately replaced its review queue with per-account registers, and this does not bring the queue back — a row is simply flagged until something looks at it.

sections.heading: What is in the set
sections.text: Only rows that arrived unattended: - transactions imported from the feed ; - transfers Purser merged automatically ; - replacements produced by a rule ; - adjustments Purser posts when you reconcile an account, whoever asked for the reconcile. Your own imports are not included. A QIF or CSV file you chose to import is not something you need reminding to review, so a 6,000-row Quicken import adds nothing to the set. Neither do rows your agent writes: each is attributed to its token in the audit log and marked agent-made in the register. Upcoming rows a schedule expects are not in it either. An expected bill or paycheck is a forecast, not something that happened; when the bank row it predicted arrives, that row is the one to review. Everything that existed before this feature shipped counts as reviewed, so it starts quiet and only ever concerns rows that arrive from now on.

sections.heading: Rows leave the set on their own
sections.text: You usually do not have to mark anything. A row clears when anything you or your agent does touches it : editing it, posting it, confirming a transfer, confirming a match or matching it to an expected row by hand. The action is the review. Automation is different. A rule that recategorizes a row, the nightly categorization pass, or a match Purser confirms on its own leaves it needing review — automation touching a row is not the same as someone checking it. That is the whole point of the flag. A review follows the bank line . When a pending row you reviewed (or confirmed a match on) posts, the posted row arrives already reviewed — who reviewed it, when, the note and any flag come along — as long as it carries the same category you saw on the pending. If the posted row lands in a different category, it needs review again, because that category is something nobody has looked at. A row the bank posts after you never reviewed its pending stays in the set. A merged transfer is a new judgement of its own, so merging rows into a transfer never carries their review.

sections.heading: Working through it
sections.text: In the UI, unreviewed rows carry a needs review badge in their register, and the dashboard shows how many are outstanding. Both come from the same server-side check, so they always agree. Over the REST API, each row from GET /transactions (and a single transaction's detail) carries it as needs review; read that rather than treating a missing reviewed at as unreviewed, because rows outside the set never get a mark. From an agent, review batch returns the next rows with everything needed to judge them inline — current category and who chose it, any transfer on the row, the raw-versus-friendly payee, what automation did — plus a short checklist. There are no per-row round-trips by design; a reviewer that has to fetch context row by row will skip it. Then mark reviewed closes the loop, in bulk and idempotently.

sections.heading: Check what context was available
sections.text: Every batch reports a context map saying which surfaces it could actually offer. If something a decision needed was unavailable, that batch's rows were reviewed with less information than they look like they had — so the guidance says to escalate rather than clear in that case.

sections.heading: Escalating
sections.text: A reviewer that is unsure can mark a row reviewed and flag it for you. The row leaves the unreviewed set — no second queue appears — but shows a flagged badge and carries a note explaining why. The clearest case is an ambiguous transfer: categorizing a row as [account path] names an account, not a specific row, so when two rows in that account could be its pair, the right move is to hand it back rather than guess.

sections.heading: Letting Purser review it for you
sections.text: If you have configured an AI provider, you can have the review pass run server-side instead of waiting for a connected agent. It is off by default and needs its own switch — configuring a provider grants nothing on its own. When enabled, it runs after each sync, clears what the context supports, and escalates the rest, so your attention lands on the residue rather than the whole set. It is capped per run, and a provider failure simply leaves rows unreviewed rather than breaking the sync. Rows it clears are recorded as ai review, permanently distinguishable in the audit trail from a row you looked at yourself.

sections.heading: Nothing grows forever
sections.text: If reviewing lapses, rows older than PURSER REVIEW MAX AGE DAYS (90 by default) are auto-marked as aged by a nightly sweep. That is deliberately a different mark from a real review, so an audit reader can always tell which rows were actually examined — and the count is reported in your digest rather than clearing silently, because the sweep firing at all means review has lapsed.

sections.heading: Fixes that repeat should become rules
sections.text: The checklist ends with this and it is worth repeating: if you find yourself making the same correction over and over, that is a rule waiting to be written. These flags are the record of what your rules did not catch. See Write deterministic rules.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: - Write deterministic rules - Manage transfers - DESIGN.md section 4 (review marks) and decision 47

pages.title: Write deterministic rules
pages.description: Categorize, rename payees, and declare transfer pairs with rules that run automatically on new transactions — and never execute until you activate them.

sections.text: Rules are deterministic instructions Purser runs where automation already touches your rows: at import, and in the nightly sweep. They decide, so they are deliberately boring — no regex, no scoring, no fuzzy matching. A rule either matches or it does not, and you can read why off a single line. There are three kinds: - categorize — set a category, or name another real account to convert the row into a transfer, when a rule matches. - rename — map a raw bank descriptor to a friendly payee. - transfer link — declare that two accounts transfer to each other.

sections.heading: A rule never runs until you activate it
sections.text: A rule is created as a draft unless the call that creates it sets activate. Drafts are visible, editable and previewable, but they do not execute — the loader that feeds the import and sweep paths only ever selects active rules. An agent creates rules as drafts too, unless you asked it for the rule: then it may create it already active (propose rule with activate=true). A rule that is the agent's own idea stays a draft for you to decide. A pair (transfer link) rule is always created as a draft, because its activation confirms how many past pairs it will link (see below). Every rule write — creating, activating, editing or reaching back into history — needs the write scope and is recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Preview before you activate
sections.text: The predicate is the part worth checking, so preview it against your real history first: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/preview \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"match field": "payee", "match mode": "contains", "match text": "amazon"}' You get back how many live rows match, how many were scanned, and a sample. A count far larger than you expected is the signal that the predicate is too broad — narrow it with an account, an amount range, or a direction. A transfer link rule previews the same way, with its account pair instead of a predicate (see Declaring a transfer pair).

sections.heading: Matching is token-aware, not substring
sections.text: Text matching normalizes both sides and respects token boundaries, so a rule for an account named Chase does not fire on PURCHASE RETURN. Three modes: mode matches --- --- equals the whole normalized text prefix starts with the pattern, ending on a token boundary contains the pattern as a whole run of tokens prefix with star matches star market but not starbucks coffee. This makes a prefix rule useful for bank descriptors whose stable payee text is followed by a changing bill number or reference.

sections.heading: Everything you set is ANDed
sections.text: A predicate is the AND of whatever fields you set; unset fields are unconstrained. You can scope by account, by amount (amount exact, or an amount min/amount max range), by direction (debit or credit), and by effective from, which excludes rows dated strictly before it. direction reads the amount after any per-account sign inversion, so you write the rule in your sign world, not the bank's.

sections.heading: Which rule wins
sections.text: Rules of one kind are evaluated in priority order — lower numbers first — and the first match wins . GET /rules returns them in exactly that order, so resolution is visible before it fires rather than being something you deduce afterwards. Priority is a number you set, not something Purser infers from how specific a rule looks. That is on purpose: a rule's effect should be explainable by pointing at one row.

sections.heading: Map a payee durably
sections.text: For a durable payee mapping, use a categorize rule with match field: payee and choose the narrowest safe text mode. Its action target may be a virtual category such as expenses.utilities, or a real account such as liabilities.auto loan; a real target uses the same bracket-transfer conversion as an inline edit. Rules are the only automatic mapping from payee text that you configure, and they come first. Payee memory and the AI classifier (next section) only fill in rows no rule matched, and neither is a mapping you can edit. Nothing in the suggestions inbox applies a mapping itself either: the most a suggestion can do is propose one as a rule, which you accept through the same activation as a rule you write. That includes transfers: confirming a transfer by hand teaches Purser no hidden payee-to-account mapping — it proposes a transfer link rule (see A pair scoped to a payee).

sections.heading: Rules beat learned memory
sections.text: For categorization the order is: rule, then payee memory, then the AI classifier, then uncategorized A rule sits above the payee-to-category memory learned from your accepted history, so a rule can correct a memory that has gone wrong. If you find yourself fixing the same categorization repeatedly, that is the signal to graduate it into a rule.

sections.heading: Renaming consolidates history, not just new rows
sections.text: A rename rule rewrites the payee , never the bank's description — three different identity checks read that description, so rewriting it would corrupt them. Applying a rename to history does not rewrite your transactions. It aliases the payee itself, pointing the raw payees at the friendly one. Nothing about any posted row changes, and because payee memory counts rows across the whole alias group, consolidating several descriptors onto one payee makes that payee's memory stronger for everything that already happened. Clearing the alias undoes it.

sections.heading: Declaring a transfer pair
sections.text: Purser already links transfers automatically when the text carries a signal — a keyword like transfer or payment, or the counterparty account's name. Some real transfers carry neither. Recurring brokerage moves often arrive as opaque descriptors on both sides. A transfer link rule declares the account pair, and for that pair the name-signal requirement no longer applies. Everything else still does : the amounts must be exactly opposite, the two dates must fall inside the pair's window, both rows must be posted, and a pair you explicitly unlinked stays unlinked.

sections.heading: The pair's date window
sections.text: By default the two sides of a declared pair must post within 3 days of each other — the same window every other pair uses. Some transfers take longer: a card autopay that leaves checking on the 1st and lands on the card on the 5th is 4 days apart, and would stay unlinked. Set window days on the rule to give that pair, and only that pair , its own window: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"type": "transfer link", "pair account a": "CHECKING ID", "pair account b": "CARD ID", "amount exact": "184.50", "window days": 5}' - window days is a whole number of days from 0 (same day only) to 14. Leave it out for the standard 3 days. A value outside that range, a fraction, or a window days on any other kind of rule is refused with a 422. - It combines with amount exact and effective from, which narrow the pair as before. - A window below 3 narrows the pair: the rule vouches only for legs that post that close together. A name-signal pair still links within the standard 3 days, as it would without the rule. - A wider window never takes a row from a closer pair already in your ledger. Each pass first links everything inside the standard 3 days exactly as it would without the rule, and only then pairs the declared accounts farther apart, among the rows still without a partner. Every pair you did not declare keeps the 3-day window. Keep the window as narrow as the bank's real delay. Exact opposite amounts are the only other evidence a declared pair needs, and a wide window gives a stray equal amount more room to pair with the wrong row. A pair that repeats weekly should not go past 3.

sections.heading: A pair scoped to a payee
sections.text: A pair rule can be narrower than the whole pair. When you confirm a transfer by hand, Purser proposes a transfer link rule for those two accounts that only applies when one side of a pair carries the confirmed payee — see From a confirm to a rule. Accepting the suggestion creates that rule as a draft. Its predicate then reads a leg's payee is "..." or an alias, and GET /rules and MCP list rules show the payee as payee scope. Pairs between the same accounts with any other payee still need a name signal or a confirm. The scope follows the payee's aliases . When a rename's apply-history points the scope's payee at a friendlier one, or points other descriptors at it, rows under any payee in that group are covered and the rule shows the payee under its current name. A rename only merges payees through apply-history, and apply-history only aliases the payees of live rows. A payee whose rows have all been merged into transfers is not aliased, and neither is one whose rename only ever ran on new rows. Rows under the new name then fall outside the scope; confirm one of those pairs and Purser proposes a rule for the new name. The payee scope is part of what an active rule links, like its window: an active rule refuses an edit that would drop or change it. Rules you write yourself declare the whole pair; a payee scope comes from an accepted suggestion. Preview a pair before you create the rule: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/preview \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"pair account a": "CHECKING ID", "pair account b": "CARD ID", "window days": 5}' The answer's links is how many historical pairs such a rule would link, and sample shows a few of them with their dates and gap days.

sections.heading: Activating a pair rule
sections.text: Because the nightly sweep looks at all of your posted history, activating one of these applies it retroactively. Purser therefore tells you how many historical pairs it would link — with the rule's own window — and asks you to confirm that number: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/$RULE ID/state \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"state": "active", "confirm links": 12}' The count is computed by the same selection the sweep then runs, so it is the number that links: pairs of one-sided rows merged into a transfer, and rows absorbed into an existing transfer that was waiting for its other side. It matches what the preview above reported for the same history. The confirmation is not ceremony. Merging two rows is balance-neutral, so the post-sync balance check that catches most mistakes cannot see a wrong one — every balance stays correct while two unrelated rows are silently one. The count is your check instead. Use effective from to bound it, or narrow window days, if the number looks high. An active pair rule cannot be edited in a way that changes what it links (the pair, amount exact, effective from, window days or its payee scope): the edit is refused. Disable the rule, edit it, and activate it again, so a wider scope goes through the same confirmation. The Applied column on the Rules page (applied count on GET /rules, applied in the MCP list rules tool) counts how many times a rule has fired. A pair rule counts each link it makes, merged pairs and absorbed rows alike, including the links the nightly sweep makes after you activate it. A categorize or rename rule counts each new row it shapes, and a run over history counts once. Previews and the confirmation count above never add to it, and unlinking a transfer does not take a count back.

sections.heading: Applying a rule to history
sections.text: New rules do not quietly rewrite the past. POST /rules/{id}/apply-history is the only path, and it is a dry run unless you say otherwise: curl -sX POST https://purser.example.com/rules/$RULE ID/apply-history \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PURSER TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"dry run": true}' The dry run's counts are the real run's results — both walk the same candidate list. That list covers all of your history, however long: the preview samples the newest 5,000 rows (scan capped says when it stopped there), but apply-history examines every live row and reports how many as scanned. By default it touches uncategorized rows and rows automation categorized, and leaves anything you categorized alone; overriding your own choices is opt-in. Posted rows are skipped unless you ask for posted: "correct", which mints a proper reversal and replacement for each one. A categorize rule never touches a transfer, which has no category to set — not even with include user categorized. Transfers its predicate matches are left out of matched and reported as skipped transfers. Rows in a different currency from the rule's category are left out the same way and reported as skipped currency: a transaction keeps one currency. Split transactions (one bank amount across several categories, from a QIF import) are read-only and left out the same way, reported as skipped splits. transfer link rules have no apply-history: the nightly sweep is their retroactive application.

sections.heading: From an agent
sections.text: Three MCP tools mirror this: list rules shows the active set in evaluation order, preview rule dry-runs a predicate, and propose rule creates one: a draft, or an active rule with activate=true when you asked the agent for it. There is no MCP tool to activate a draft later; that happens on the Rules page or over REST. For a pair, pass pair accounts (two account paths) to preview rule and propose rule, with an optional window days. The preview's links is the count the activation will ask you to confirm, and list rules shows each pair rule's window days and, for a payee-scoped one, its payee scope. An agent may also accept a transfer-link suggestion with decide suggestion: that creates the rule as a draft; activating it confirms its projected link count, on the Rules page or over REST.

sections.heading: See also
